Its name, also spelled Kachchh, means a land that alternates between wet and dry stages, such as the Rann of Kutch that makes up much of the district. Outside of the summer monsoon season, riverine features like the Kadiya Dhro gorge in our photo typically dry up. Also known as 'India's Grand Canyon,' Kadiya Dhro draws visitors whether or not its stream is flowing—but when it is, take care if you're tempted with a swim, as crocodiles have been spotted in the murky flow.

windows-spotlight-12059.jpg.title: Ocean coral reef beach waves
windows-spotlight-12059.jpg.headline: Joyous Réunion
windows-spotlight-12059.jpg.description: Roughly oval in shape, the overseas French territory of Réunion is lapped by the Indian Ocean on all sides. Here near the westernmost edge of this 970-square-mile isle, wide shelves separate the sandy shoreline from the wave break by as much as a quarter mile, leaving a long, calm stretch of shallows that's great for casual swims and dazzling snorkel sessions alike. Along with its fellow islands in the Mascarene chain, Réunion is one of the world's best places to observe marine life, with many biologists ranking it in the top ten biodiversity hotspots on Earth.

windows-spotlight-12065.jpg.title: Ocean waves and dark rocks on sandy shore
windows-spotlight-12065.jpg.headline: Risco business
windows-spotlight-12065.jpg.description: Corral del Risco is a rugged stretch of coastline near Punta de Mita, a resort town on Mexico's Pacific coast. This aerial view captures the raw beauty of the shoreline, where waves crash against boulders smoothed by centuries of erosion. The area is part of the Riviera Nayarit, a region known for its biodiversity, luxury resorts, and traditional fishing villages. The rock piles here are remnants of ancient lava flows, and the surrounding waters are rich with marine life, making this a popular area for snorkeling and diving. If you'd rather stay on dry land, Punta de Mita itself sits on a peninsula that offers panoramic views of Banderas Bay and the Marietas Islands.

windows-spotlight-12067.jpg.title: São Miguel das Missões Ruins, São Miguel das Missões, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil
windows-spotlight-12067.jpg.headline: A mission abandoned
windows-spotlight-12067.jpg.description: Though its architecture is distinctively European, a peek at palm trees through this ruin's outer door hints at its wild New World setting. São Miguel das Missões was one of several missions established by the Jesuit order in the late 1600s near the triple frontier of Brazil, Argentina, and Paraguay. The missions' mission? To 'civilize' the local Guaraní people by bringing them into planned Catholic communities—an effort that only lasted until Spain expelled the order from the Americas in 1767. The missions' melding of Catholicism with Indigenous ways shaped the lasting culture of the region, with UNESCO recognizing several of the ruins (including São Miguel) as World Heritage Sites.

windows-spotlight-12068.jpg.title: Crescent City Connection, New Orleans, Louisiana
windows-spotlight-12068.jpg.headline: Bridging the Big Easy
windows-spotlight-12068.jpg.description: Although more than 20 miles of the Mississippi River wind past the city of New Orleans, only one bridge spans the mighty river within city limits. Well, really it's two. The twin spans of the Crescent City Connection, one westbound and one eastbound, connect central New Orleans with the city's 15th Ward. Better known as Algiers, this southeastern segment of the city packs a lot of history, having transformed from a hub of the slave trade to a unique center of African American and Creole culture—especially music. Brass bands first paraded the streets here in the 1870s, and numerous Algiers-born musicians were instrumental in the creation of jazz.

windows-spotlight-12070.jpg.title: Pelješac Cable-Stayed Bridge, Sunset, Pelješac, Croatia
windows-spotlight-12070.jpg.headline: Shortcut over the sea
windows-spotlight-12070.jpg.description: Until recently, reaching the cut-off corner of Croatia we see in the distance required doubling around a long, narrow bay, plus a double border crossing at the Herzegovinian coastal strip of Neum. That potentially hours-long ordeal is cut to about a 5-minute drive by the Pelješac Bridge, which spans roughly a mile and a half across this Adriatic inlet. The project was a political hot potato for years due to its potential limiting of shipping to Neum. But the pro-bridge crowd won out in the end, and the span was completed in 2022, recording 2 million crossings in its first year.

windows-spotlight-12073.jpg.title: Forth Bridge steel railway bridge sunset, Queensferry, Scotland
windows-spotlight-12073.jpg.headline: Span of steel
windows-spotlight-12073.jpg.description: Sounding like the makings of a tongue twister, the Firth of Forth is one of Scotland's most important bodies of water, bordering the country's capital Edinburgh near its opening to the North Sea. A little further west, the hill-bounded inlet (the word 'firth' relates to the Nordic 'fjord') narrows as we approach the Forth River. In 1882, engineers settled on this crossing—previously served by ferries—to build the Forth Bridge silhouetted in our sunrise shot. Ambitious for its time, it was the first large structure in Britain built from steel, and when completed, it boasted the longest main cantilever span in the world (today second only to Canada's Quebec Bridge).

windows-spotlight-12085.jpg.title: Paraglider over Sand Dunes
windows-spotlight-12085.jpg.headline: Dunes for days
windows-spotlight-12085.jpg.description: The Namib Desert, one of the world's oldest and driest, stretches along Namibia's coast in a mesmerizing expanse of golden dunes. Near the coastal town of Swakopmund, thrill-seekers take to the skies for a bird's-eye view of this surreal landscape. Paragliding here offers a unique perspective on the desert's shifting sands and stark beauty. From high above the dunes, you might even spot the desert wildlife that make this harsh locale home, such as ostriches and oryxes.

windows-spotlight-12094.jpg.title: Infinity pool, city skyline, sunset, Panama City, Panama
windows-spotlight-12094.jpg.headline: A canal-centered capital
windows-spotlight-12094.jpg.description: Panama City's skyscraper-packed skyline would stick out anywhere, but it's especially striking in this part of the world: In terms of height, Panama's photogenic capital includes the top 50-plus buildings in Central America. The city's long-ongoing construction boom owes mostly to its position at the Pacific end of the globally important Panama Canal, making it a hub of world finance and shipping logistics. Since 1999, when the Panamanian government assumed full control of the Canal Zone, Panama City has also become a top tourism destination. Hundreds of luxury hotels dot the metropolis—many with infinity pools like this one capitalizing on the capital's stunning sea-meets-mountains setting.

windows-spotlight-121.jpg.title: Spiral Grass Paths, Sydney
windows-spotlight-121.jpg.headline: A spiral in Sydney
windows-spotlight-121.jpg.description: If you're not dizzy by the time you reach the top of this hill, the 360-degree view is well worth it. The artificial mound and spiral path are a high point of Sydney Olympic Park, the sprawling complex built for the Australian metropolis' summer hosting stint in 2000. So it's been some time since the park served as the world's epicenter of athleticism, but it's still loved by locals as a great place to jog, swim, birdwatch, disc golf, see public art, enjoy community gatherings, and more.

windows-spotlight-12107.jpg.title: Blue Collared Kingfisher
windows-spotlight-12107.jpg.headline: An avian angler
windows-spotlight-12107.jpg.description: Equipped with sleek, sharp beaks great for spearing or plucking up prey, the bird family called kingfishers lives up to its name. But that prey doesn't always come from the water: In fact, many kingfisher species are spread over a wide range of biomes both wet and dry, often relying more on bugs and worms than a seafood diet. This blue-breasted kingfisher was spotted in the Gambia, a river-centric country where surf and turf are both on the menu.

windows-spotlight-12114.jpg.title: Turquoise tide, brown rock formations, tide pools, ocean waves
windows-spotlight-12114.jpg.headline: Turquoise tide
windows-spotlight-12114.jpg.description: Here in northwestern Australia's Kimberley region, turquoise waters meet ancient rock formations, some over 1.8 billion years old. The circular pools scattered across this craggy surface were formed by the relentless action of waves and weather over millennia. The Kimberley is known for its dramatic tides—some of the largest in the world at almost 40 feet—which shape the coastline daily. These waters also support a rich marine ecosystem, including dugongs, sea turtles, humpback whales, and fish by the school. On land, the Kimberley is a lot less crowded: It's home to only about 34,000 people in an expanse the size of California, with vast areas of wilderness accessible only by boat or small aircraft.

windows-spotlight-12116.jpg.title: Dolomite Peaks, Lake Misurina Village, Dolomites, Italy
windows-spotlight-12116.jpg.headline: Peaks over the 'Pearl'
windows-spotlight-12116.jpg.description: The glassy surface and gentle hues of Lake Misurina are reflective of its fancy nickname: the Pearl of the Dolomites. The multi-peaked mountain ridge called Sorapiss frames this view toward the lake's southwest edge (do an about-face and you'll get a peek at the famed peaks of Tre Cime di Lavaredo). Most of Misurina's lakeshore is lined with lux resorts and restaurants, but the multi-story building in our photo's center is historically a clinic for treating childhood asthma—taking advantage of this microclimate's immaculate Alpine air.

windows-spotlight-12122.jpg.title: Bronze-toned dome building at sunset
windows-spotlight-12122.jpg.headline: A bronze-toned dome
windows-spotlight-12122.jpg.description: As the Church of Santo Domingo de Guzmán stuns with its incredibly intricate baroque facade, a demure dome next door sidesteps the spotlight. Featuring simple shapes and muted terra cotta tones, this 17th-century compound at the center of San Cristobal, Chiapas, is a former convent built by the Dominicans—a Catholic order from Seville, Spain, where the architecture is rich in Arabic influence. Today, the convent is home to two museums and a center for traditional Mayan textiles, a mixed role that reflects Chiapas' convergent cultures.

windows-spotlight-12123.jpg.title: Eye-shaped sandy island with paddleboard
windows-spotlight-12123.jpg.headline: An eyelike isle
windows-spotlight-12123.jpg.description: The United States' biggest border city with Mexico is famously a feast for the eyes, and this peeper-shaped island is just one of San Diego's hidden-in-plain-sight nature havens. Mission Bay is the centerpiece of the largest human-made aquatic park in the nation at 6.6 square miles, over half of which is water. A former wetland converted to a shallow tidal inlet, it's a haven for jet skis, sailboats, and kayaks—and paddleboards like this one parked on Leisure Island, a tiny landmass also reachable by trail during especially low tides.

windows-spotlight-12125.jpg.title: Sellicks Beach colorful cliffs white sand turquoise ocean, South Australia
windows-spotlight-12125.jpg.headline: This beach is packed
windows-spotlight-12125.jpg.description: Tucked between rugged hills and open ocean, this strip of South Australia beach is something of a local parkway. The hard-packed sand is suitable for driving, and pleasure cruises are a common pastime—though most folks just park their vehicles to enjoy the seaside for a spell. Four-wheel drive may be ideal here, but Sellicks has an especially rich history with two-wheelers, hosting its first motorcycle race as early as 1917 and later holding yearly time trials. This event stalled out by the mid-1950s, but recent revivals have seen dozens of vintage bikes make tracks on the beach.

windows-spotlight-12126.jpg.title: Vancouver City Skyline Night Reflection, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada
windows-spotlight-12126.jpg.headline: A seabound skyline
windows-spotlight-12126.jpg.description: The central core of British Columbia's biggest city is packed onto a small peninsula, squeezing over 60,000 city-slicker Canadians into a skyscraper-covered area of just 1.5 square miles. That's only half the size of this sea-surrounded strip of land. Downtown Vancouver occupies the peninsula's southern portion, while here on the north side you'll find yourself in Stanley Park, the flagship of Vancouver's vast array of green spaces. Attractions like beaches, pavilions, and a miniature railway are found along the park's seawalled edges, and hiking trails allow visitors to venture off the paved path. But don't get lost in the woods: Belying its urban setting, Stanley Park's center is a thick, wild forest, with some of its centuries-old Douglas firs and western redcedars rising over 200 feet tall.

windows-spotlight-12137.jpg.title: Hin Ta Hin Yai Rocks, Koh Samui, Thailand
windows-spotlight-12137.jpg.headline: Anyone for gulf?
windows-spotlight-12137.jpg.description: Take a look at Thailand on a map and you'll see a narrow 'tail' of land separating the Gulf of Thailand from the Andaman Sea. The two bodies of water stand in sharp contrast: The deep, wild Andaman has a mean depth of more than 3,500 feet, while the warm, turquoise-tinted Gulf averages under 200. Just offshore from both coasts, hundreds of islands dot the seas: We're on the shores of Ko Samui (the nation's second-largest island after Phuket)—a touristy locale known for seaside granite formations and gorgeous waterfalls.

windows-spotlight-12138.jpg.title: Antelope Canyon, Page, Arizona
windows-spotlight-12138.jpg.headline: Sacred sandstone
windows-spotlight-12138.jpg.description: One of the most popular tourist attractions in the roughly 17.5-million-acre Navajo Nation, Antelope Canyon is both a natural wonder and a cornerstone of local culture. Over millions of years, rose-red sandstone walls have been eroded into flowing, ethereal shapes. The site is traditionally sacred to the Navajo, and access is limited to excursions led by tribal guides—partly to ensure respect for the canyon as a cultural site, and partly to protect guests from flash floods, which can arise quickly in this arid area prone to monsoon rains.

windows-spotlight-12139.jpg.title: Purple Pasque Flowers
windows-spotlight-12139.jpg.headline: Petals of purple
windows-spotlight-12139.jpg.description: The genus Crocus includes about 100 species spread across Eurasia and North Africa. You might spot purple crocus blossoms like these as early as February here in Germany—even peeking through frost or light snow. Other species of crocus may feature white or yellow flowers, and some bloom in the late summer or fall. One autumn bloomer, the also-purplish Crocus sativus, is particularly valuable: Its bright red stigmas, better known as saffron once dried, are the most expensive spice in the world by weight and must be delicately hand-picked.

windows-spotlight-12141.jpg.title: Teal and Terracotta Art Deco Building, Southern California
windows-spotlight-12141.jpg.headline: A SoCal throwback
windows-spotlight-12141.jpg.description: Home to only about 100,000 people at the turn of the 20th century, Los Angeles was a metropolis of a million and a half by 1940. Since the city's huge growth spurt happened amid the heyday of Art Deco architecture, many of its iconic structures incorporate this lavish, geometric style: City Hall, the Eastern Columbia Building, Griffith Observatory, the gilded movie houses along Broadway, and more. By the postwar period, Art Deco had mostly fallen out of the mainstream. But some modern developments in the ever-growing City of Angels pay homage to the bygone style, like this ornamental arch overlooked by looming palms.

windows-spotlight-12143.jpg.title: Stony shores
windows-spotlight-12143.jpg.headline: Stony shores
windows-spotlight-12143.jpg.description: Located within India's Khangchendzonga National Park along the strenuous Goecha La trek, Samiti Lake sits at 13,800 feet above sea level, offering a rest stop with reflective views of the surrounding heights. Khangchendzonga (more often spelled Kangchenjunga) is the third-highest mountain in the world after Mount Everest and K2, and many of the summits that form its impressive massif are visible from Samiti's shores. It may be tough to turn one's gaze downward on this peak-packed route, but it's worth it: Rhododendrons bloom throughout the park in the spring, and wildlife like red pandas and Himalayan black bears roam the forests.

windows-spotlight-12144.jpg.title: Zebra stripes
windows-spotlight-12144.jpg.headline: Stripe science
windows-spotlight-12144.jpg.description: Why do zebras have stripes? As far as science is concerned, the answer's not in black and white. Originally, it was thought that stripes camouflage the animals amid tall savanna grasses like those found here in Tanzania. But other research has suggested they serve as an illusion for predators,as reflective protection from hot sunlight, or even as a visual bug repellent. One thing we do know: Stripes help us identify zebras by species—like this Grant's zebra, recognizable by the stripes across its belly—and even as individuals, since their stripe patterns are unique, just like human fingerprints.

windows-spotlight-12147.jpg.title: Clownfish Anemone
windows-spotlight-12147.jpg.headline: Buddy picture
windows-spotlight-12147.jpg.description: The ocellaris clownfish is a common component of a colorful coral reef scene, usually sharing the shot with its symbiotic sidekick, the sea anemone. Thanks to a special mucus layer on its skin, the clownfish is immune to the normally stinging anemone, which provides the fish shelter in exchange for food scraps, parasite cleanup, and a little muscle to ward off anemone-hungry butterflyfish. While stripey orange is certainly the most widely known clownfish coloration (we're looking at you, Nemo), ocellaris clownfish also appear in a sleek black and white, as well as a spotty, splotchy pattern popularly called the Picasso.

windows-spotlight-12149.jpg.title: Teal Golden-hooded Tanager
windows-spotlight-12149.jpg.headline: A teal-tinted tweeter
windows-spotlight-12149.jpg.description: Tanagers are the second-largest bird family in the world, making up about 4% of all bird species, but most types of tanager are endemic to particular regions of Central and South America. The green-headed tanager's only home is here in the Atlantic Forest, a vast bioregion stretching from Brazil into corners of Paraguay and Argentina. Thanks in part to protected reserves and corridors, birdwatchers can spot these dazzling flyers throughout the forest—often even in city parks and gardens.

windows-spotlight-12150.jpg.title: Black-winged Stilts criss-cross kiss, shallow water, golden hour
windows-spotlight-12150.jpg.headline: A criss-cross kiss
windows-spotlight-12150.jpg.description: Needle-like beaks, pointy tail feathers, and long, spindly legs give the black-winged stilt quite the sharp look. And a familiar one: Wading birds of the genus Himantopus can be spotted on shorelines all over the world. Black-winged stilts—for example, this courting pair photographed in France—often breed in the northern parts of Eurasia and Africa before migrating south for the winter. Due to their great adaptability and range, some biologists group them with stilts of the Americas and Oceania to form a single cosmopolitan species.

windows-spotlight-12152.jpg.title: Desert rock formation, tilted tree, sunset
windows-spotlight-12152.jpg.headline: Rigid rock, tilted tree
windows-spotlight-12152.jpg.description: Amid the stark, windswept beauty of Joshua Tree National Park, a twisting juniper and a teardrop-shaped boulder make a striking duo. Junipers are hardy evergreens that thrive in arid climates, often living for hundreds of years. Their berries (actually seed cones rather than true berries) are a food source for birds and mammals, and their knotty trunks tell stories of survival in harsh desert conditions. An even more ancient tale is told by Joshua Tree's geology, which includes monzogranite formations sculpted by wind and water over millions of years.

windows-spotlight-12153.jpg.title: Blue Common Kingfisher
windows-spotlight-12153.jpg.headline: Fishies beware
windows-spotlight-12153.jpg.description: Bright plumage and pinpoint hunting skills make the kingfisher family a favorite among birdwatchers worldwide. The common kingfisher can be spotted across Europe, Asia, and North Africa, usually as it dives after swimming prey in an electric-blue flash. At rest—like this specimen seen in Germany—kingfishers are usually silent and still as they perch above the water, patiently scanning for passing fish. When they're not seen at all, it could signal a problem with the ecosystem: Due to their high sensitivity to water quality, kingfishers are considered indicator species.

windows-spotlight-12156.jpg.title: Illuminated Toronto skyline with CN Tower at night, Toronto
windows-spotlight-12156.jpg.headline: Toronto glow
windows-spotlight-12156.jpg.description: Toronto, Canada's largest city, stretches along the northwestern shore of Lake Ontario, offering a stunning skyline view from across the water. The city, with a population approaching 3 million, is characterized by a mix of modern skyscrapers, residential towers, and green spaces near the lake's edge. Dominating the skyline is the CN Tower, a concrete communications and observation tower with a distinctive tapered shape designed for stability and wind resistance. Rising 1,815 feet tall, it remains one of the tallest freestanding structures in the world and a true icon of this lakeside cityscape.

windows-spotlight-12161.jpg.title: Stratified Martian mud patterns
windows-spotlight-12161.jpg.headline: Of Mars and mud
windows-spotlight-12161.jpg.description: To reach the layered clay mounds known as the Bentonite Hills, you'll need a solid, high-clearance off-road vehicle. And if it rains, good luck: The mud that forms in these monsoon-touched Utah uplands could get a monster truck stuck. Speaking of risk-fraught excursions, not far from here, a rotating cast of experts prep for a different sort of wild journey. The Mars Desert Research Station operates nearby as an analog habitat, simulating challenges a settlement on Mars might face. Small groups of scientists, journalists, and others perform simulated missions in this environment that, during the winter cold, is thought to closely resemble conditions on the Red Planet.

windows-spotlight-12170.jpg.title: Diverse Green Delta White Birds
windows-spotlight-12170.jpg.headline: A diverse delta
windows-spotlight-12170.jpg.description: The Gediz Delta is one of the largest wetlands in Türkiye and one of its 14 Ramsar sites, recognized for its high biodiversity. During the winter, it provides a rich habitat for as many as 80,000 birds from hundreds of species. The most multitudinous is Phoenicopterus roseus, shown here in a flock of several dozen wading the delta's waters. Known more familiarly as greater flamingos, the spindly, pinkish-white flyers rule the roost in this riverine land, with around 15,000 breeding pairs calling the Gediz region home.

windows-spotlight-12172.jpg.title: Pair of Red-headed Sarus Cranes
windows-spotlight-12172.jpg.headline: Extra-large lovebirds
windows-spotlight-12172.jpg.description: Sarus cranes are the tallest flying birds in the world, often reaching nearly 6 feet in height. Native to the Indian subcontinent, these cranes are known for their elaborate courtship dances and trumpeting mating calls. Sarus pairs mate for life, and in Indian mythology they symbolize love and fidelity, and their presence is considered a sign of good luck and a healthy ecosystem. Despite their cultural importance, sarus cranes are listed as vulnerable due to habitat loss. This crane couple has found a safe haven here in Jim Corbett National Park, India's oldest national park and a refuge for more than 600 animal species.

windows-spotlight-12173.jpg.title: Glacial Lagoon Icebergs Sunset, Jökulsárlón, Iceland
windows-spotlight-12173.jpg.headline: Where 'bergs are born
windows-spotlight-12173.jpg.description: As the ice caps around it have slowly shrunk, the iceberg-laden lake known as Jökulsárlón has only grown wider and deeper. The lake began forming in the 1930s as meltwater filled the recesses left by Breiðamerkurjökull glacier, which began retreating in the 19th century. In recent decades, glacial melting has kicked into high gear, reportedly doubling Jökulsárlón in size from the 1990s to the mid-2000s. Though its growth is a reminder of threats facing glaciers worldwide, it's rightfully a popular attraction: Visitors are often lucky enough to witness the 'birth' of icebergs as they calve off Breiðamerkurjökull and splash into the open water.

windows-spotlight-12175.jpg.title: Painted Stork soaring with green foliage
windows-spotlight-12175.jpg.headline: A stork soars
windows-spotlight-12175.jpg.description: This still shot of a painted stork was snapped in the midst of a mighty flap, scavenged shrubbery in tow. Such botanical bits and bobs are building material for the stork's nest: Despite their bulk and gangly shape, these waders raise their young way up in the trees, often in colonies of hundreds alongside other waterbirds like herons and pelicans. Of course, with their 3-foot-plus stature, hooked orange beaks, and 'bald' heads, painted storks stick out even in the most crowded of tree canopies.

windows-spotlight-12181.jpg.title: Longjing Tea Rings with Green Tree, Hangzhou
windows-spotlight-12181.jpg.headline: Longjing rings
windows-spotlight-12181.jpg.description: Centuries of careful cultivation have earned this ancient city its clout as China's 'tea capital.' Here in Hangzhou, layer after labyrinthine layer of verdant shrubbery is terraced along steep hills. Longjing tea plants are harvested early in their growth cycle, then pan-roasted to remove the leaves' water and bring out complex flavors. Local legend says the best cup of Longjing is brewed with a secret ingredient: water from the natural Hupao Spring, located nearby.

windows-spotlight-12183.jpg.title: Roman Amphitheater Arcade, El Jem, Tunisia
windows-spotlight-12183.jpg.headline: Arcade of antiquity
windows-spotlight-12183.jpg.description: This interior snapshot brings us to an ancient, open-air arcade—but you won't need a fistful of quarters here. In architectural terms, 'arcade' refers to any long row of arches—in this case, the uppermost of three tiered arcades that partly encircle the El Jem Amphitheatre. Built in the 3rd century CE by the Romans, the Amphitheatre seated as many as 35,000 spectators, making it one of the largest arenas in the empire despite its remoteness. Its stacked arcades offered standing room for droves of gladiator fans, as well as walkways to wander and stretch the legs.

windows-spotlight-12189.jpg.title: Rippled Sand Beach Sunset Bird, Belgium
windows-spotlight-12189.jpg.headline: Beach life in Belgium
windows-spotlight-12189.jpg.description: A solitary seabird sails over streaked sands and North Sea waves at this Belgian beachfront. Part of the province of West Flanders, Belgium's coast is set some distance from inland population centers like Bruges and Antwerp—so despite the many mid-rise resorts lining the beaches, the seaside retains an out-of-the-way feel–especially here in De Haan, a town known for its preserved Belle Époque villas that make for a low-slung skyline.

windows-spotlight-12192.jpg.title: River Canyon, Texas
windows-spotlight-12192.jpg.headline: Of tectonics and Texas
windows-spotlight-12192.jpg.description: Santa Elena Canyon's walls put the 'Big' in Big Bend National Park as they stretch 1,500 feet into the blue Texas sky. This desert landscape feels as old as time, but it's relatively young geologically: Most formations here result from rough-and-tumble tectonics within the past 100 million years. The resulting tossed and turned bedrock was later eroded by the (even younger) Rio Grande, forming deep gorges whose sediment layers lie at various odd angles. The canted cliffs in this shot are just a hint at the park's extreme elevation differences: More than 6,000 feet separate Big Bend's highest and lowest points.

windows-spotlight-12194.jpg.title: Coastal sand dunes golden grass ocean sunset, Highlands, Scotland
windows-spotlight-12194.jpg.headline: A Highland haven
windows-spotlight-12194.jpg.description: The phrase 'Eigg, Muck, and Rùm' rings a bit like a Scottish delicacy, à la rumbledethumps, cullen skink, or neeps and tatties. Indeed, the trio are a feast for the eyes from this beach in the Highlands. They're the three Small Isles visible from Camusdarach Beach, an outpost of soft, white sand in Scotland's rural Lochaber region. Set several hours' drive from big cities like Glasgow and Edinburgh, the site nonetheless sees plenty of summer visitors seeking vast views and a dip in the crystal-clear waters. A portion of these pilgrims are drawn by film fandom: Scenes from the acclaimed movie 'Local Hero' were shot on location at Camusdarach.

windows-spotlight-12195.jpg.title: Green Karst Hills Rice Paddies
windows-spotlight-12195.jpg.headline: Infinite hills
windows-spotlight-12195.jpg.description: Many provinces throughout Vietnam are favorite tourist destinations, but some are still remote enough to remain relatively undiscovered. Cao Bang is a sort of hidden treasure, a highland province in the northeast of the country bordering China's Guangxi Province. It's said that roughly 90% of Cao Bang's area is made up of heavily forested mountains, and you can see a great example of that mostly vertical landscape in our image. Rice fields are frequently found where the land is flat, and on hillsides as well. Along with all the greenery comes some splashes of blue—the province is home to Ban Gioc Falls, one of the most beautiful cascades in the country.

windows-spotlight-12199.jpg.title: Concrete bridge, snowy islands, turquoise ocean, winter, Storseisundet Bridge, Norway
windows-spotlight-12199.jpg.headline: Concrete connection
windows-spotlight-12199.jpg.description: Numerous nooks and countless crannies make Norway's coast one of the longest in the world. Vast fjords and narrow channels divide islands and peninsulas in all directions, and this complex geography calls for a lot of land connections. Concrete cantilever bridges—like this one, the more southerly of the twin Fredvang Bridges—are commonplace not just in archipelagic areas like here in Lofoten, but all over Norway. Their prevalence began in the postwar period when steel was scarce, leading Norwegians to advance the use of prestressed concrete for short, strait-hopping spans.

windows-spotlight-1220.jpg.title: Nugget Point Lighthouse, The Nuggets sea stacks, South Island coast, Nugget Point, Otago, New Zealand
windows-spotlight-1220.jpg.headline: Warning: Nuggets
windows-spotlight-1220.jpg.description: One glance at those rocks scattered in the ocean around Nugget Point illustrates just why a lighthouse was built on this New Zealand outcrop. The rugged Otago coast may be beautiful, but woe betide the sailor who bumps their boat into its many seabound stones. Not too surprisingly, these surf-tossed islets just off Nugget Point are called the Nuggets. Visitors can get a good view of them, and possibly a nearby gathering or two of fur seals, from the viewing platform in front of the lighthouse.

windows-spotlight-12201.jpg.title: Haystack Rock, Needles, Tidal Pools, Sunset, Cannon Beach, Oregon
windows-spotlight-12201.jpg.headline: Needles and a haystack
windows-spotlight-12201.jpg.description: Of the many rugged formations lining the 362-mile Oregon Coast, Haystack Rock might be the best known. Standing 235 feet from sand to summit, it's one of the tallest sea stacks in the United States, and the surrounding beach (dotted with smaller stacks known as the Needles) is a favorite for sunset strolls and tide pooling. Lovers of '80s cinema already know Haystack's main claim to fame: 'The Goonies,' where it makes a memorable backdrop to a ragtag group of kids' quest for pirate treasure. Standing a short walk from downtown Cannon Beach, the rock is about 25 miles south of Astoria—the Goonies' hometown in the film and Oregon's oldest city.

windows-spotlight-12204.jpg.title: Bow Fiddle Rock sea arch, sunset, Portknockie
windows-spotlight-12204.jpg.headline: Rocky Portknockie
windows-spotlight-12204.jpg.description: Pareidolia is the term for noticing familiar faces and shapes in natural phenomena, and it comes up often in the naming of rock formations like this one off Portknockie, Scotland. This 50-foot chunk of quartzite poking above the North Sea waves is said to look like the very tip of a violin bow, lending it the name Bow Fiddle Rock. And what about 'Portknockie'? That naming history is a little less straightforward: The Gaelic word chnocaidh, meaning hill, became 'knockie' through anglicization.

windows-spotlight-12206.jpg.title: Lake Plateliai, green forests, golden fields, Plateliai
windows-spotlight-12206.jpg.headline: High over Plateliai
windows-spotlight-12206.jpg.description: A peninsular plain juts out from the town of Plateliai into the lake of the same name—the largest here in the Samogitia region of northwestern Lithuania. Most of the nation's several thousand lakes are located at the opposite end of the country in the Baltic Highlands, so this 3,000-acre lake is a local treasure. It's also the centerpiece of Žemaitija National Park (named for an alternate spelling of Samogitia), an 84-square-mile protected area that includes the lake, the town, and the surrounding wilderness of thick forests and boggy wetlands.

windows-spotlight-12210.jpg.title: Sea Cave, Sea Stack, Ocean Waves, Olympic National Park, Washington
windows-spotlight-12210.jpg.headline: Olympic-size views
windows-spotlight-12210.jpg.description: While the main section of Olympic National Park protects woods and rainforests deep in Western Washington's interior, a long, narrow exclave of the park lines the state's sparsely populated Pacific coast. Chilly and stormy throughout most of the year, this unique corner of the United States becomes a rare treat for those who venture here in the warmer months. In addition to stunning sea stacks and shoreside rock formations, visitors can appreciate a plethora of wildlife like seabirds, otters, and tide pool-dwelling marine critters—all protected under the Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary, which spans most of Washington's outer shores.

windows-spotlight-12211.jpg.title: Misty Lake Mountain Twilight Reflection
windows-spotlight-12211.jpg.headline: Where's Fuji?
windows-spotlight-12211.jpg.description: We wanted to show you a picture of Japan's tallest mountain, but nature had other ideas. While Lake Shōji is one of the Fuji Five Lakes—each renowned for a unique, postcard-perfect view of Mount Fuji—misty conditions like this often obscure the famous peak. Still, the early-morning fog itself makes for a fine photo, and the calm, cool conditions also lend themselves to another popular pastime here: fishing. Lava flows from Fuji formed rocky outcrops that stick out at various spots on Lake Shōji, making fine perches for hopeful anglers.

windows-spotlight-12214.jpg.title: Orange Lenticular Cloud over Snow-capped Mountain Peaks at Sunset, Torres del Paine National Park, Patagonia, Chile
windows-spotlight-12214.jpg.headline: Saucer spotted?
windows-spotlight-12214.jpg.description: Set those phasers back to stun, space cadets—false alarm. Turns out this 'mothership' caught on camera over southern Chile is just a very large lenticular cloud. Often said to look like alien spacecraft, these strangely shaped clouds may have contributed to early reports of UFO sightings. They form as directional winds hit obstacles like mountains or tall buildings, forcing air upward until it cools and its moisture condenses, then sinks back down to its previous level and evaporates. This cycle continues throughout the (usually quite short) life of the cloud, so while lenticulars appear stationary, they're actually in constant flux.

windows-spotlight-12216.jpg.title: Red Sunset Sky Low Tide Pools
windows-spotlight-12216.jpg.headline: A low-tide tableau
windows-spotlight-12216.jpg.description: Between its renowned stretches of sunny, sandy beach, San Diego's shores are lined with steep cliffs and ocean-battered rock beds. Many of the pits and crevices worn into the stone remain filled with water at low tide, making fine habitats for anemones, starfish, sea slugs, and other small marine creatures. This popular patch of tide pools is located just below the cliff-bounded La Jolla neighborhood, home to a major underwater wildlife reserve and the West Coast's oldest oceanography institute.

windows-spotlight-12217.jpg.title: Angkor Wat Temple Sunset, Siem Reap, Cambodia
windows-spotlight-12217.jpg.headline: Stories etched in stone
windows-spotlight-12217.jpg.description: Angkor Wat has been an important Buddhist center through most of its nearly 900-year history, so why is it covered in stone-carved scenes of Hindu mythology? The complex was built in 1150 CE under king Suryavarman II, a devotee of the Khmer Empire's traditional Hinduism. Within just a few decades—two kings and an enemy invasion later—the new Buddhist monarch Jayavarman VII began rededicating the temple to his own religion. Though some Hindu elements were removed, many remain: Bas-reliefs depict multitudes of apsaras and other Hindu figures, covering more than 12,000 square feet of the structure.

windows-spotlight-12224.jpg.title: Keyhole Arch Solstice Sunbeams, Pfeiffer Beach, Big Sur, California, USA
windows-spotlight-12224.jpg.headline: Solstice sunbeams
windows-spotlight-12224.jpg.description: While West Coast Christmases are seldom white with snow, nature finds other ways to get in the holiday spirit here in the Golden State. A landmark of the Big Sur region south of Monterey, California, Keystone Arch puts on a seasonal light show each year. Peaking in late December near the winter solstice, the effect occurs when the setting sun lines up just right with Keystone's through-cut sea cave—as permitted by the persistent NorCal winter fog.

windows-spotlight-12227.jpg.title: Orange Coastal Desert Sand Dunes
windows-spotlight-12227.jpg.headline: A bone-dry coast
windows-spotlight-12227.jpg.description: Blue sea and sky create a two-tone tableau with warm-hued sands in what may be the world's oldest desert, and that's not the only sharp contrast you'll discover here. Daytime temperatures in the Namib regularly tip above 100 degrees Fahrenheit, while nights can dive below freezing. And while the inland of this sandy strip—which covers Namibia's entire seaboard—is one of the driest places on the planet, moist mists gather offshore to hug the high-slung coastal dunes, summing up to as many as 180 foggy days a year. This northerly section of the Namib is nicknamed the Skeleton Coast for the many shipwrecks its low-visibility conditions have caused.

windows-spotlight-12228.jpg.title: Green Island and Yellow Kayaker at Sunset, Finland
windows-spotlight-12228.jpg.headline: Afloat in Finland
windows-spotlight-12228.jpg.description: Popular on rivers, lakes, and seas all over the globe, kayaks originated with the seal-hunting Indigenous peoples of Greenland and northern Canada. While we're a good ways from the fjords and floes of the Arctic Ocean, this kayaker is exploring a region also noted for its hardy, cold-ready folk. Known as Sápmi, the northernmost region of Finland is home to the Sámi people, who historically fished the waters here at Lake Inari. Among the more than 3,000 islands on the lake, a few host ancient Sámi cultural sites, including a major burial ground and a stone islet thought to have been used for sacrifices.

windows-spotlight-1223.jpg.title: Gosausee, wooden dock, sunrise fog, mountain peaks, Salzkammergut, Austria
windows-spotlight-1223.jpg.headline: A sight worth its salt
windows-spotlight-1223.jpg.description: The lake called Vorderer Gosausee lies still under a misty summer sunrise in our striking shot. This area of Austria was once known not so much for scenery as salt production: Unfortunately for many folks from the Bronze Age and beyond, they spent a lot of their time hunkered in salt mines rather than watching the sun sweep over the Alps. But nowadays, most denizens of the Salzkammergut region are lucky enough to ply their trades above ground, with the dramatic surroundings as a perk.

windows-spotlight-12232.jpg.title: Callanish Stones, Milky Way Night Sky, Isle of Lewis, Outer Hebrides, Scotland
windows-spotlight-12232.jpg.headline: Of circles and stars
windows-spotlight-12232.jpg.description: Seeing outer space from this stone circle on the outskirts of Scotland, it's easy to imagine prehistoric people gazing at the same shooting star-filled sky in ages long past—and we're not even sure how long. It's estimated that the standing stones of the Ring of Brodgar were placed between 4,000 and 4,500 years ago, but precisely dating the site has proved difficult even with modern methods. Digs on the Ness of Brodgar—the wider UNESCO site that includes the ring—have revealed dozens of structures as old as 5,500 years, so after decades of study there are still more questions than answers about its age. Not to mention its purpose—though like other stone circles, especially its southerly cousin Stonehenge, it's hypothesized to have been a tool for ancient astronomers.

windows-spotlight-12237.jpg.title: Angkor Wat Temple sunrise reflection, Siem Reap, Cambodia
windows-spotlight-12237.jpg.headline: An emblematic temple
windows-spotlight-12237.jpg.description: Angkor Wat is such a stalwart symbol of Cambodia that its shape has graced the country's flags for over a century, even through long periods of political turmoil. Considered the largest religious building in the world, the Hindu-turned-Buddhist temple has stood in this spot since the 12th century, carefully aligned east to west to match the sun's motion. The temple's distinctive five central towers—arranged in a symmetrical pattern called a quincunx—represent Mount Meru, the mythic five-pointed peak where the Hindu gods reside.

windows-spotlight-12239.jpg.title: Snowy Owl yawning dune
windows-spotlight-12239.jpg.headline: 'Who' you laughing at?
windows-spotlight-12239.jpg.description: Seems like this snowy owl thinks you're quite the hoot. Whether it's having a chuckle or a yawn, this wise flyer is right at home pretty much anywhere there's a chill in the air. While most common in snow-prone places like Canada, Russia, and Scandinavia, snowies have been spotted wintering as far south as the Gulf Coast of the United States. In addition to being well-traveled, these birds are notably long-lived: The oldest known wild specimen, originally banded in Massachusetts in the 1990s, was last seen at the ripe avian age of 23.
windows-spotlight-12239.jpg.copyright: © Vicki Jauron, Babylon and Beyond Photography/Moment/Getty Images

windows-spotlight-12241.jpg.title: Palma Cathedral night reflection, Palma, Mallorca
windows-spotlight-12241.jpg.headline: An island sanctuary
windows-spotlight-12241.jpg.description: Though its full designation is the Catedral-Basílica de Santa María de Mallorca, this landmark of the Balearic Islands' capital is more often called Palma Cathedral. The city of Palma's 438,000-plus locals shorten the name further still, preferring the two-syllable La Seu (Catalan for 'the seat,' from the same Latin root as the Holy See). By any name long or short, the cathedral and its neatly rowed Gothic spires are one of the most famous sights of Mallorca, and that's just the view from outside. Step inside the sanctuary and you'll be treated to the grandeur of a 145-foot-high nave, illumined in rich color by the second-largest rose window in the world.

windows-spotlight-12244.jpg.title: Tree at sea orange sunset
windows-spotlight-12244.jpg.headline: A tree at sea
windows-spotlight-12244.jpg.description: Though located all the way across the Bay of Bengal from the mainland, the tiny Andaman and Nicobar Islands account for more than a quarter of India's coastline. Comprising 836 isles and islets that arc about 500 miles from north to south, the archipelago's tangled shores are largely lined with mangroves: saltwater-loving trees whose sinuous roots reinforce the shoreline's structure and help reduce erosion. The term 'mangrove' refers to about 60 plant species that share these traits, and more than half of them can be found in the Andamans' saline shallows and swamps.

windows-spotlight-12246.jpg.title: Ipanema Beach, Two Brothers Mountain, Rio de Janeiro
windows-spotlight-12246.jpg.headline: The view from Ipanema
windows-spotlight-12246.jpg.description: The name Ipanema comes from a Tupi term meaning 'stinking water,' but that hasn't kept it from becoming a byword for beauty. Stunningly set on the open Atlantic in the city's southeast, this Rio de Janeiro neighborhood inspired the sultry bossa nova tune 'The Girl from Ipanema,' one of the most recorded pop songs of all time. Ipanema isn't the only local waterfront with a song title tie-in: The next beach over is the famous Copacabana, namesake of the notable nightclub memorialized by Barry Manilow.

windows-spotlight-12248.jpg.title: Wind-rippled Turquoise Ocean, Volcanic Rock Coast, Tropical Trees, Distant Island Mountain, Maui, Hawaii
windows-spotlight-12248.jpg.headline: Blue water, blowing wind
windows-spotlight-12248.jpg.description: In terms of shape, Maui is sort of a lopsided figure-eight: two roughly circular shield volcanoes separated by a narrow land strip. The active Haleakalā makes up three-fourths of the landmass, while the extinct Mauna Kahālāwai (better known as the West Maui Mountains) forms the western quarter. Except for the low-lying isthmus joining the two, as well as the broad Central Valley at Haleakalā's base, the island's population mostly lives in small cities hugging the rugged coast, connected by ring roads that circle the dual massifs. Our vantage point is in swanky Wailea, one of several resort towns along the Haleakalā side's southwest shore. Across the azure expanse of Māʻalaea Bay, we can see the Kaheawa Wind Power project's 34 wind turbines spinning on the West Mountains' gust-prone slopes.

windows-spotlight-12249.jpg.title: Silhouetted Sea Stacks Sunset, Bandon Beach, Oregon
windows-spotlight-12249.jpg.headline: Silhouetted stacks
windows-spotlight-12249.jpg.description: Not far from the westernmost point in Oregon, Bandon Beach is home to one of the most eclectic sea stack assortments on the 362-mile Oregon Coast. Made of volcanic basalt exposed by geologic uplift and sculpted by wave erosion, the stacks come in all shapes and sizes here—from the twisting Wizard's Hat (this photo's main subject) to the distant Cat and Kittens Rock (partly visible on the horizon) to the looming, 72-foot-tall Face Rock. Run out of stone shapes to count? Look to the sands: From April to August, a local nonprofit called Circles in the Sand draws elaborate labyrinths on the beach each morning.

windows-spotlight-12251.jpg.title: Red paraglider, Snow mountains, Alpine
windows-spotlight-12251.jpg.headline: Alpine altitude
windows-spotlight-12251.jpg.description: Sightseeing in the Alps often demands driving through winding, narrow mountain passes, cramming into cable cars, or strapping on crampons to tramp up slippery slopes. So in this elevated section of Switzerland, flight equals freedom—as our paraglider pilot pal is experiencing firsthand. We're only getting a small slice of their panoramic view, which includes more than just mountains. Beneath the thick snow below, the mighty Aletsch Glacier snakes between the steep Bernese Alps, forming the largest ice mass in the Alpine countries.

windows-spotlight-12252.jpg.title: Arctic coastal bridge, snow-capped mountains, Lofoten Islands, Norway
windows-spotlight-12252.jpg.headline: An Arctic archipelago
windows-spotlight-12252.jpg.description: At any time of the year, the Lofoten archipelago is a fantastic panorama of craggy peaks, steep cliffs, scattered islands, and gem-like water. The scene gets even more unearthly when autumn and the first snows arrive. Cod fishing is still a key industry here in the Lofoten area of northwestern Norway, but tourism is a growing trade, even after the summer crowds have departed. A series of bridges (one of which is seen in our image) connect the area's small, isolated fishing villages, and they also help visitors explore this extraordinary landscape no matter the season.

windows-spotlight-12257.jpg.title: Vestrahorn mountains, black sand beach, sunset, Stokksnes
windows-spotlight-12257.jpg.headline: Sunset at Stokksnes
windows-spotlight-12257.jpg.description: Vestrahorn rises dramatically from Iceland's southeastern coast, its hornlike peaks accenting the black volcanic sand of Stokksnes Beach. Composed of ancient gabbro and granophyre, the massif is one of the few in Iceland made from intrusive igneous rock rather than surface lava. The Stokksnes headland is a favorite spot among photographers for its moody skies and mirror-like reflections, and it also holds cultural significance: Vestrahorn figures prominently in local folklore as well as on Icelandic postage stamps.

windows-spotlight-12259.jpg.title: A two-legged tower
windows-spotlight-12259.jpg.headline: A two-legged tower
windows-spotlight-12259.jpg.description: Crashing waves from the wide-open Atlantic Ocean continually carve the sandstone coast of Orkney, the small island chain just off Scotland's northern tip. The exposed striations here at Yesnaby, on the west edge of Orkney's main island, show how Devonian sediment layers were built up and compressed at odd, often zigzagging angles before being revealed by erosion. The effect is especially visible on Yesnaby Castle, the stilted sea stack at our photo's center. Rising about 115 feet, the crooked 'castle' is a popular target for intrepid climbers, despite its seemingly precarious posture on two legs.

windows-spotlight-12260.jpg.title: European Bee-eaters with wings spread in wildflower meadow
windows-spotlight-12260.jpg.headline: A bug's bane
windows-spotlight-12260.jpg.description: The colorful plumage, the winter layovers in the tropics—who doesn't love the European bee-eater? Bees. Bee-eaters really do eat bees, and other insects as well. They catch bugs midair, carry them to a perch, and pound them to rub out most or all of the venom, making them safe to eat. You can find these jewel-toned birds throughout much of Europe, especially in nature reserves and parks. It's easy to see why they're a favorite subject of photographers, whether perching, flying, hunting, or (as it seems here) bragging about their daily haul of bees.

windows-spotlight-12267.jpg.title: Hilltop Branik Castle, Branik, Slovenia
windows-spotlight-12267.jpg.headline: The bastion of Branik
windows-spotlight-12267.jpg.description: Known either by its old German name Rihemberk, or as Branik Castle after the modern Slovenian town nearby, this rebuilt keep is the latest of many to grace this hilltop. First fortified by the Romans, the site became home to a series of aristocratic families, with its oldest records dating to the 1200s. The complex's owners reshaped and added to it continually as it changed hands over the centuries—but World War II brought this to an end as the Partisans dynamited and severely damaged the castle. Yugoslavia nationalized the site after the war, but rebuilding wouldn't begin until the 1980s—and despite the castle's current polished look, some of its prewar profile is still missing.

windows-spotlight-12275.jpg.title: Red Blue Filaments Nebula
windows-spotlight-12275.jpg.headline: A celestial creepy-crawly
windows-spotlight-12275.jpg.description: A spider with 3-light-year-long legs seems like awfully bad news for arachnophobes, but if you're one of the 6% of Earth's population afflicted with fear of spiders, rest assured the Red Spider Nebula can't get you. Big as this bug is, it's also far away: a nice, safe distance of roughly 5,000 light years. And the legs? Just massive, bubble-like dust clouds inflated by gases that billow from the central white dwarf. Appropriately, this spidery shot was captured by NASA's Webb Telescope, whose Near-InfraRed Camera (NIRCam) makes finely detailed imaging possible from astronomical distances.
windows-spotlight-12275.jpg.copyright: © ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, J. H. Kast

windows-spotlight-12276.jpg.title: Sailboat Ocean Rocky Coast Sunset
windows-spotlight-12276.jpg.headline: Sailing into sunset
windows-spotlight-12276.jpg.description: Check out the western coast of Türkiye on a map (or chart, if you happen to be on a boat) and you'll find a long, tangled line defined by countless promontories and peninsulas. Additionally, the adjacent Aegean Sea is specked with numerous islands, making for a mélange of straits, channels, inlets, and bays that's a playground for sailors. Our photo subject, sailing westward into the sunset, is on course for an international journey: Most of the larger islands in these parts belong not to Türkiye but its seaward neighbor Greece.

windows-spotlight-12291.jpg.title: Coastal Bluffs and Beach, Pacific Ocean, Point Reyes National Seashore, California
windows-spotlight-12291.jpg.headline: A seafarer's stopover
windows-spotlight-12291.jpg.description: At this spot about 30 miles from San Francisco, Drakes Bay washes up on the breaker-battered Drakes Beach, as Drakes Estero drains into the bay behind us and Sir Francis Drake Boulevard brings a flow of fellow visitors. So what's with all the Drake? In 1579, halfway through circling the globe, the English sea captain Francis Drake brought his ship aground for repairs right here at Point Reyes National Seashore. It's said that these pale, sandy slopes reminded Drake and company of the Cliffs of Dover, and crew journals indicate the Coast Miwok people hosted the homesick sailors here for more than a month.

windows-spotlight-12293.jpg.title: Blue Icebergs, Glacial Lake, Mountains
windows-spotlight-12293.jpg.headline: Where blue bergs bob
windows-spotlight-12293.jpg.description: The saga of this backcountry lagoon is large in scope, beginning with Iceland's biggest glacial mass and ending in the wide open ocean. The ice cap of Vatnajökull, which covers 8% of the island nation's area, includes dozens of outlet glaciers whose meltwater flows into various streams, rivers, and lakes. 932-foot-deep Jökulsárlón is the endpoint of Breiðamerkurjökull, an outlet glacier that—like the rest of Vatnajökull—has long been shrinking. As a result, these waters have grown: Since glacial retreat revealed the lake in the 1930s, its placid surface and blue icebergs have come to fill a 5-mile gap between the glacier and a short, narrow channel to the Atlantic.

windows-spotlight-12299.jpg.title: Patchwork agricultural fields, volcanic cones, ocean, Terceira Island
windows-spotlight-12299.jpg.headline: A Terceira aerial
windows-spotlight-12299.jpg.description: This sweeping shot highlights a patchwork of farmland stitched among small volcanic cones: a quintessential view of Terceira, one of nine major islands in the Azores archipelago. Dormant calderas and craters provide fertile soil throughout the Portuguese island chain, making agriculture a central part of Azorean life. That even includes the twin Cabras Islets in the distance, once home to goatherds who tended livestock there ('cabras' means 'goats' in Portuguese).

windows-spotlight-12303.jpg.title: Blue starry cave night
windows-spotlight-12303.jpg.headline: A night-lit niche
windows-spotlight-12303.jpg.description: Thanks to its skylight-pocked ceiling, moon and sun alike have a straight shot at the floor of this Middle Caicos cave. Seen here bathed in the eerie blue of a lunar long-exposure shot, Indian Cave is a place of strange beauty by night or day—the vinelike ficus roots that dangle from its ceiling only add to the fantasy-novel feel. These unique features may single Indian Cave out, but caverns and sinkholes are commonplace across the Turks and Caicos Islands, owing to the territory's limestone bedrock that's prone to erosive karst action.

windows-spotlight-12306.jpg.title: Golden sand beach, towering cliffs, ocean waves, Kauai, Hawaii
windows-spotlight-12306.jpg.headline: Garden Isle grandeur
windows-spotlight-12306.jpg.description: The westernmost publicly accessible point in Hawaii happens to be on the state's longest beach, which curves 17 miles around the leeward side of Kaua'i. We use 'accessible' loosely here, though: You'll want a sturdy off-road vehicle for the journey to Polihale State Park, a 2-mile portion of the beach reached by a rough, tough-to-maintain dirt road. Travelers who brave the ridges and ruts will find a peace that's increasingly rare on the trendy Garden Isle, and with the proper camping permits, there's no need to limit the stay to one day. But don't count on any snorkeling or surfing: Save for a few short stretches, rip currents make these open seas unsafe for swimming.

windows-spotlight-12311.jpg.title: Dunas de Concón, Valparaíso, Chile
windows-spotlight-12311.jpg.headline: Sand dunes and salty air
windows-spotlight-12311.jpg.description: Though the arid Atacama starts its long, sandy stretch some distance north of here, the Concón Dunes form a sample-size desert right here in the big city. Valparaíso, formerly the principal port of this elongated nation, anchors one of the largest metro areas in Chile, where dry inland air meets the open Pacific for mild Mediterranean weather year-round. The climate combined with the city's rich hillside architecture, including a system of 16 funiculars, makes Valparaíso a popular tourist stop—helping compensate for the shipping industry slowdown that started way back when the Panama Canal opened.

windows-spotlight-12317.jpg.title: Strait of Messina, Italy
windows-spotlight-12317.jpg.headline: The strait story
windows-spotlight-12317.jpg.description: This overview of Italy's busy Strait of Messina is one of countless finely detailed images available in the Microsoft Planetary Computer. This vast, cloud-powered database lets scientists see a whole timeline of crisp satellite captures and environmental data for any location in the world. By analyzing this data, scientists can explore better ways to manage land and water resources, combat climate change, and prepare for natural disasters. Here at Messina, for example, an observer could trace the strait's strong tidal currents over time to note effects on the coastal ecosystem, or track patterns in the various boat routes crisscrossing the bridgeless waterway.

windows-spotlight-12327.jpg.title: Interacting Galaxies
windows-spotlight-12327.jpg.headline: A cosmic crossing
windows-spotlight-12327.jpg.description: A streak of space dust and gas crosses the enormous gulf between two dwarf galaxies that whirled close together hundreds of millions of years ago, then drifted an incredible distance apart. NGC 4490, the larger of the two (whose diffuse light is seen at the image's left edge), long ago captured a mass of nebular material from its then-neighbor NGC 4485 (seen as a loose star cluster at the upper right). As the galaxies separated, this mass was stretched into an astronomically long trail. The resulting intergalactic bridge is a breeding ground for stars: peppered throughout its span are regions of heavy ionization from new star clusters, blazing neon blue in this near-infrared shot from the James Webb Space Telescope.
windows-spotlight-12327.jpg.copyright: © ESA/Webb, NASA & CSA, A. Adamo (Stockholm University), G. Bortolini, and the FEAST JWST team

windows-spotlight-12328.jpg.title: Blue Orange Nebula, Stardust, Stars
windows-spotlight-12328.jpg.headline: A pawful of stardust
windows-spotlight-12328.jpg.description: Though our stable Solar System is now thousands of light years from any star-forming action, we humans have understood the basics of how stars are born since at least the days of Immanuel Kant. In 1755, he suggested that clouds of space matter slowly gathered into very dense clumps, eventually becoming heavy enough to form the sun and later the planets. Called the nebular hypothesis, this is still the best-supported model of how planetary systems form, and it appears all across the universe. This image—captured by the James Webb Space Telescope—details the Cat's Paw Nebula, an active stellar nursery over 4,000 light years away.

windows-spotlight-12329.jpg.title: Snowy Mountains Purple Sunset Reflection, Scotland
windows-spotlight-12329.jpg.headline: Snows of Scotland
windows-spotlight-12329.jpg.description: Reflecting meringue clouds with the sugar-frosted Cairngorm Mountains as a backdrop, Loch Morlich is a sweet spot in this Scottish wilderness. During this time of year, Cairngorms National Park can feature some of the harshest winter weather in Britain, its high plateaus given to heavy snows and sudden weather shifts. While a few larger lochs lie among the park's distant peaks, Loch Morlich is especially popular for its easy access and broad shape, which make it a hotspot for watersports like windsurfing when weather permits.

windows-spotlight-12330.jpg.title: Stone Arch Bridge and Traditional Pavilion, Lijiang
windows-spotlight-12330.jpg.headline: Lovely Lijiang
windows-spotlight-12330.jpg.description: Today a modern, diverse city of more than a million people, Lijiang's history of human habitation stretches back as far as 100,000 years. In that context, the series of dynasties that built the city's renowned Old Town were just drops in time's pond, each lasting just a few centuries. But they made their mark on the land—especially the Ming Dynasty, which left Lijiang with a sophisticated system of canals built to supply water for drinking, bathing, and irrigation. Fed by the Black Dragon Pool seen here, the waterways snake amid tangled, touristy streets packed with gable-roofed traditional homes.

windows-spotlight-12335.jpg.title: Green Terraced Rice Fields with Farm Hut
windows-spotlight-12335.jpg.headline: Nice rice
windows-spotlight-12335.jpg.description: Rice is the main staple food for more than half the people on Earth, and Indonesia is far from an exception. The fourth-most populous country in the world is also its fourth-largest rice producer, cultivating the miniscule cereal grains on a massive scale to the tune of 55 million tons. Like in many hilly rice-producing regions, the paddies are arranged in stepped terraces, so rainwater flow and gravity do much of the irrigation work. Here in Bengkulu Province, Sumatra, many farmers have adopted a resource recycling system involving livestock: Their cattle eat straw made from the rice plant's grassy blades, and the inevitable manure fertilizes the fields.

windows-spotlight-12336.jpg.title: Flume Gorge, Franconia Notch State Park, New Hampshire
windows-spotlight-12336.jpg.headline: Let's trek it up a notch
windows-spotlight-12336.jpg.description: If you wondered how the Granite State got its nickname, you'll find no better object lesson than Franconia Notch State Park. Chock full of Conway granite cliffs and crags, the Notch is one of the most important passes through the White Mountains, which cover about a quarter of New Hampshire. On this lush summer's day, we're strolling the Flume Gorge trail, a 2-mile loop showcasing 90-foot granite walls rising over the churning Flume Brook and Avalanche Falls.

windows-spotlight-12342.jpg.title: White seal pup flippered facepalm, sandy beach
windows-spotlight-12342.jpg.headline: A flippered facepalm
windows-spotlight-12342.jpg.description: Tradition here in Britain says to keep a stiff upper lip, but we all get overwhelmed sometimes—just ask this seemingly world-weary grey seal pup. It's possible the little paddler is just a bit hangry. After they're weaned off their mother's fat-rich milk, young grey seals spend a few weeks fasting before they hit the high seas to hunt their own fishy prey. Once they do, though, it's a whole new set of pinniped problems: predator threats, competition with other seals, human-made obstacles like fishing nets, and the list goes on. Buckle up, pup: Grey seals have been noted to live over 40 years, so you're in for a long ride.

windows-spotlight-12343.jpg.title: Protostar L1527 surrounded by nebulous matter
windows-spotlight-12343.jpg.headline: Feeding a future sun?
windows-spotlight-12343.jpg.description: Some say stars are born, not made—and while that may apply to showbiz, in space it's a bit more complicated. Star formation is a long process of accumulating material bit by bit, condensing molecular clouds into extremely dense clumps that finally collapse into a protostar. This near-infrared image from the James Webb Space Telescope is centered on protostar L1527, showing the nebulous matter it's drawing in from multiple directions via gravity—'feeding' on the gases and dust to grow larger. You may need to squint to see it, but that darker line bisecting the brightest point of the protostar is a protoplanetary disk: a ring of orbiting matter that could be the beginnings of a new planetary system.

windows-spotlight-12348.jpg.title: Snow-capped Mountains, Elevated Reservoir Sunset, Bernina Pass, Switzerland
windows-spotlight-12348.jpg.headline: An elevated reservoir
windows-spotlight-12348.jpg.description: When it's well fed by the surrounding glaciers, Lago Bianco looks like most any other alpine lake, but in drier times, its divided past is revealed. Prior to the 20th century, this stretch of the Bernina Pass hosted a much smaller Lago Bianco alongside its sister lake, Lago della Scala. In 1910, engineers began damming the basin at both ends, soon merging the lakes into one large reservoir to power hydroelectric plants in the valleys below. That year proved formative for this elevated sector of Switzerland, also marking the completion of the Bernina Pass railway—the highest rail crossing in Europe.

windows-spotlight-12350.jpg.title: Fishing harbor, red rorbuer, snowy mountains, Hamnøya
windows-spotlight-12350.jpg.headline: The haven of Hamnøya
windows-spotlight-12350.jpg.description: You might need your keyboard set to Norwegian to write home about this sleepy corner of Europe where Festhæltinden peak looms over Hamnøya harbor, just up the road from a village known only as Å. Despite the Lofoten region's maritime focus, with fishing villages and marinas set on islands large and small, cars are the main mode of transport around here. The Lofoten Mainland Connection, completed in 2007, offers an express route to Å via an impressive series of bridges and tunnels, including (if you'll allow us one more special character) the 2-mile-long Sløverfjord submarine tunnel.

windows-spotlight-12351.jpg.title: Moorland Valley Fog Sunrise, Dry Stone Wall, Windswept Tree, Peak District, United Kingdom
windows-spotlight-12351.jpg.headline: A writer's wonderland
windows-spotlight-12351.jpg.description: A wind-worn tree, a dry-stone wall, and a misty infinity in the distance—does this scene strike a note of poetry for you? Then you're in good company, as England’s Peak District has inspired holders of the pen for centuries. Many scholars pinpoint places mentioned in Arthurian legend to locales within this national park, and poets like William Wordsworth and authors like Jane Austen referenced the district in their works. More recently, literary adaptations like 'Pride and Prejudice' and 'The Princess Bride' have showcased the Peaks' pastoral landscape in cinema.

windows-spotlight-12352.jpg.title: Jungle-covered rock islands, tropical beach, ocean waves
windows-spotlight-12352.jpg.headline: A pint-sized paradise
windows-spotlight-12352.jpg.description: While it isn't the largest national park in this Central American country, it may be the most beautiful: Situated on less than 8 square miles of land, Costa Rica's Manuel Antonio National Park is a slice of central Pacific coast heaven. The nature reserve was established in 1972 to preserve the area from commercial development. Instead of beachfront resorts and souvenir shops, visitors will find four pristine beaches—some dotted with greenery-topped sea stacks—and accessible hiking trails traversing the thick rainforests that carpet the hills above the coastline. The park is an example of how big of an impact a small amount of preserved paradise can make.

windows-spotlight-12354.jpg.title: Blue Ice Formation Talking Blues
windows-spotlight-12354.jpg.headline: Talking blues
windows-spotlight-12354.jpg.description: Like the color of the sky, the cool blue of glacial ice results from tricks of the light. But in contrast to the Rayleigh scattering at work in the sky—where small particles deflect part of the visible spectrum before the eye can perceive it— glacier coloration happens on a molecular level. Water is composed of bonded oxygen and hydrogen, and all chemical bonds vibrate to some degree. In the case of highly compressed ice, the bonds vibrate at frequencies that cause light at the red end of the spectrum to be absorbed, never reaching the eye. Nearer the air-exposed surface of the ice, lighter or even chalk-white patches appear—an effect created by tiny air bubbles forming within the ice as it decompresses.

windows-spotlight-12355.jpg.title: Seven Coloured Earths, Chamarel Mauritius
windows-spotlight-12355.jpg.headline: Rolling rainbows
windows-spotlight-12355.jpg.description: Billowing like a tie-dyed blanket, the dune patch known as the Seven Coloured Earths adds a rainbow dusting to this already-colorful island nation. The sands are said to come in brown, red, yellow, orange, green, blue, and purple—mainly due to varying levels of iron and aluminum oxides. Though under private ownership, the field is open to the public most days with a small admission fee, and has become one of Mauritius' most popular tourist attractions. If the trip here tired you out, no worries: The surrounding village of Chamarel has a perfect climate for coffee production, and tasting tours offer sips from several growers in the area.

windows-spotlight-12358.jpg.title: Samuel Beckett Bridge night traffic, Dublin
windows-spotlight-12358.jpg.headline: Tuned for traffic
windows-spotlight-12358.jpg.description: With its simple shapes and clean lines, this River Liffey crossing is named aptly after a writer who used minimalist language to maximum effect. A swing bridge with a cable-stayed construction, the Samuel Beckett Bridge is one of more than 20 spans linking Dublin's north and south banks. Its massive harp-like pillar was delivered by barge to the site in one piece, 'strings' and all. Practical as it is elegant, the harplike shape is also a nod to the instrument's regard as Ireland's national symbol, which dates back 800 years or more.

windows-spotlight-12359.jpg.title: Badwater Basin Salt Flat, Death Valley National Park, California
windows-spotlight-12359.jpg.headline: How low can you go?
windows-spotlight-12359.jpg.description: Death Valley National Park is the largest national park in the contiguous United States, located on the California-Nevada border. It's known for being the hottest, driest, and lowest national park, with Badwater Basin marking the lowest point in North America at 282 feet below sea level. On the rare occasions that rain falls here, it accumulates over portions of the 200-square-mile salt flats. The rainwater dissolves some of the salts on the ground, then dries up, and quickly. In fact, the area is believed to have the greatest evaporative potential in the US. Rainwater doesn't stand a chance, and as it vanishes, it re-deposits salt crystals in its wake.

windows-spotlight-12363.jpg.title: Ruined Stone Château Tower on Plateau
windows-spotlight-12363.jpg.headline: Château on the plateau
windows-spotlight-12363.jpg.description: From a distance, the Fortress of Polignac seems to sprout from an impossibly huge tree stump. Rather than a petrified hunk of trunk, this plateau is actually a stout column of volcanic basalt that, from the 10th century on, has hosted a series of keeps. Before the Polignac noble family seized the spot, wood structures defended this high position. By the 14th century, the Polignacs had converted it into a stone compound with a 105-foot tower, dominating the village skyline to this day. Additions continued until the nobility met its fate in the French Revolution, after which the once-proud palace was quarried for its stone blocks. A few decades later, the Polignacs managed to buy it back, partly restoring the ruin before its designation as a historic monument.

windows-spotlight-12365.jpg.title: Kayaker Glacial Ice, Alaska Panhandle
windows-spotlight-12365.jpg.headline: A paddle in the panhandle
windows-spotlight-12365.jpg.description: On a map, the Alaska Panhandle appears as a tangled maze of straits, inlets, and fjords such as Tracy Arm—peeped here through a rift in the ice as a kayaker plies the cold water. Tracy Arm, like other fjords around the capital city of Juneau, is part of a vast network of navigable waterways that extend a thousand miles: the legendary Inside Passage. Sheltered from the open Pacific, cruise ships, ferries, shipping and fishing vessels, and even recreational craft can sail the passage all the way from Olympia, Washington, to Skagway, Alaska—and everywhere in between.
windows-spotlight-12365.jpg.copyright: © John Hyde/Alaska Stock - Design Pics/Alaska Stock/SuperStock

windows-spotlight-12366.jpg.title: Dunluce Castle ruin, Northern Ireland
windows-spotlight-12366.jpg.headline: The Red Earl's ruin
windows-spotlight-12366.jpg.description: One of many 'Game of Thrones' filming locations across Northern Ireland, Dunluce Castle has a history that sounds straight out of Westeros. Built in the 13th century by the Red Earl of Ulster, it soon became the stronghold of the McQuillan clan, lords of the coastal realm known as the Route. Through a series of battles and betrayals, the Route fell to their rivals, the McDonnells, who made Dunluce their luxury palace. But by 1690—a few lost battles and spent treasury vaults later—the destitute McDonnells abandoned the property. After centuries in ruin, it's now a United Kingdom scheduled monument—and a pop culture pilgrimage since it served onscreen (with digital additions) as Pyke, the precarious keep of House Greyjoy.

windows-spotlight-1237.jpg.title: Surfer on surfboard, pink sand beach, teal ocean waves, Bondi
windows-spotlight-1237.jpg.headline: Boarding at Bondi
windows-spotlight-1237.jpg.description: Located close to Sydney, Bondi is one of the most visited beaches in this surfing-obsessed nation, famed for frequently appearing in films and TV shows. Learn a little Aboriginal Australian and the name makes perfect sense. 'Bondi' is a word that describes foaming waves as they crash on the shore—what English speakers call surf. Of course, 'surf' is also what the enterprising sportsperson in our image intends to do as they strenuously paddle their board past the breaks, hoping for a swift ride back to shore.

windows-spotlight-12370.jpg.title: Red and white floatplane mountain lake sunset
windows-spotlight-12370.jpg.headline: We don't need roads
windows-spotlight-12370.jpg.description: Across most of the United States, traveling from town to town takes little more than hopping on the interstate. Not so in Alaska, where many communities are so remote they lack road access. The solution? Take to the skies. Whether supported by floats, skis, or sturdy tires, bush planes are the conveyance of choice for folks all over the Last Frontier. Skilled pilots make air travel possible where runways are impossible, relying on their rigs' short takeoff and landing capabilities to achieve altitude from small lakes, short land spits, and other tight spots. There are even competitions where bush pilots vie for the shortest landing stop: The best of the best can drop their craft on a dime, with the record landing measuring less than 10 feet.

windows-spotlight-12371.jpg.title: Starry Night Matterhorn Moon Lake Reflection, Switzerland
windows-spotlight-12371.jpg.headline: Moon over the Matterhorn
windows-spotlight-12371.jpg.description: On a crisp, clear enough night in the Alps, even top-biller mountains like the Matterhorn are no longer stars of the show. Europe's most famous mountain range is something of a haven for stargazers in a densely populated continent: Viewed on a light pollution map, it's an island of relatively low interference amid Western Europe's hundreds of high-population bright spots. Great viewpoints here in Switzerland are as numberless as the stars, and mirror lakes like Stellisee offer double the spectacle as they reflect stellar scenes above. Of course, a full moon can be a bit of a star spoiler—but adds its own splash of bright beauty.

windows-spotlight-12373.jpg.title: Bull Moose
windows-spotlight-12373.jpg.headline: Moose on the loose
windows-spotlight-12373.jpg.description: Considering its status as the biggest member of the deer family, it's fitting that the moose is Alaska's state mammal. Spend time here in the Last Frontier and you'll find 'big' is a common theme. This portrait of an impressively antlered bull moose was snapped in Chugach State Park, which covers an area equivalent to roughly half of Rhode Island. And it's only the second-largest of Alaska's state parks: Many miles west, the remote Wood-Tikchik State Park covers a rugged patch of wilderness just larger than Delaware.

windows-spotlight-12374.jpg.title: Sunlit Misty Autumn Forest Path
windows-spotlight-12374.jpg.headline: Witchy woods?
windows-spotlight-12374.jpg.description: The Brothers Grimm are the most famous folklorists from this part of the world, and it's no wonder so many of the tales they collected were set in moody, enchanted woods. Made up of about 90 billion trees, Germany's forests cover roughly a third of the country's land area, and many are notoriously dense and dark. The most famous example is the Black Forest near the southern border, but ample canopies can be found all over: This autumn scene was captured in the woods of Ammerland, a swampy district near the North Sea coast where beeches dominate the tree-scape.

windows-spotlight-12375.jpg.title: Blue-green forest lake, white raft
windows-spotlight-12375.jpg.headline: Of lakes and landslides
windows-spotlight-12375.jpg.description: Nestled in a dense Alpine forest and mainly accessible by foot or bike, Crestasee (aka Lake Cresta) is one of Switzerland's hidden gems. Its glassy waters shift between shades of emerald and turquoise depending on the light, mirroring the sky and surrounding evergreen forest. Most of Crestasee's water supply comes from underground sources—as is the case with many lakes in this region, where water flow was reshaped by the Flims rockslide about 10,000 years ago.

windows-spotlight-12381.jpg.title: Rhinoceros silhouette, golden sunset grassland
windows-spotlight-12381.jpg.headline: Rhinos on the rise
windows-spotlight-12381.jpg.description: Even silhouetted in early-morning savanna mists, our big-nosed buddy here is one of the most unmistakable animals on Earth. One of five extant rhinoceros species, the white rhino historically populated a large portion of southern Africa, with a northern faction living as far away as Sudan.
