By the mid-to-late 20th century they were reduced to small numbers and mainly concentrated in South Africa, but conservationists have reintroduced them to former stamping grounds like Zimbabwe, Botswana, and here in Namibia. Thanks to these efforts, more than 17,000 southern white rhinos make their home in the wild—more than the other four rhino species combined.

windows-spotlight-12384.jpg.title: Bull Moose in water, Maine
windows-spotlight-12384.jpg.headline: Of moose and Maine
windows-spotlight-12384.jpg.description: Nearly 90% covered in forest, Maine is the 'main' center in the lower 48 for moose-watching: The easternmost state is home to as many as 70,000 moose, a number beaten only by Alaska. Peak season for spotting the crepuscular creatures (that means they like to come out and feed at dawn and dusk) begins in mid-May and typically runs into July. When they aren't hiding in the deep brush, these bulkiest members of the deer family are hard to miss: Bulls can weigh in upwards of 1400 pounds. And while this hulking hoofer's velvety antlers are still sprouting, they may soon span more than 6 feet.

windows-spotlight-12385.jpg.title: Rocky coastline, green moss, tide pools, Pismo Beach, California
windows-spotlight-12385.jpg.headline: A perfect Pismo pit stop
windows-spotlight-12385.jpg.description: If you're road tripping between San Francisco and Los Angeles, the quickest route is a long, inland stretch of I-5—but where's the fun in that? If you've got all day, the scenic route is the way to go: 500 miles of the beautiful Pacific Coast Highway connect California's two biggest urban centers. Roadside attractions vary from Big Sur's stunning seaside cliffs to the dozens of charming beach communities lining the coast at sea level. This low-tide shot was taken at Eldwayen Ocean Park in the town of Pismo Beach, just a few blocks off the storied highway.
windows-spotlight-12385.jpg.copyright: © Nature, food, landscape, travel/iStock/Getty Images Plus

windows-spotlight-12386.jpg.title: Ivy-clad stone castle ruins
windows-spotlight-12386.jpg.headline: Of ruins and revolution
windows-spotlight-12386.jpg.description: A symbol of France's long-crumbled feudal legacy, this castle ruin is all that remains of fortifications that defended this spot beginning in the 10th century. First noted in Roman times by the Latin name 'segiacum castrum,' the Château de Sigy-le-Châtel grew over the following millennium as numerous nobles passed its ownership around—until one, a provincial marquis, met the guillotine during the French Revolution. Once the dust settled, private ownership of the grounds resumed and persists to this day—but most of the neglected complex was demolished around 1850.

windows-spotlight-12389.jpg.title: Yellow kayak breaking ice, frozen water patterns
windows-spotlight-12389.jpg.headline: Breaking the ice
windows-spotlight-12389.jpg.description: There's no such thing as bad weather, just bad clothes,' goes an old Scandinavian saying. Our aerial shot of an ice-defying kayaker brings us to a different part of Europe—Bulgaria, to be exact—but the aphorism applies anywhere there's a chill in the air. To a skilled and well-equipped kayaker, any body of water lacking a thick ice layer can offer opportunities for polar paddling—as our photo subject, clad in a dry suit and presumably warm layers beneath, proves by slicing a streak through the Shiroka Polyana reservoir's thin sheet of ice.

windows-spotlight-1239.jpg.title: Lalaria Beach rock arch sunset, Skiathos, Greece
windows-spotlight-1239.jpg.headline: Idyllic and isolated
windows-spotlight-1239.jpg.description: You'd think a beach this incredible would be packed to the edges with visitors, but Lalaria Beach has a barrier to entry: The Aegean Sea. This striking spot's isolated setting means you need to rent or ride a boat to reach it, so compared to many of the 60-plus beaches here on Skiathos island, getting to Lalaria can be an ordeal. Even still, Lalaria's famous rock arch and calm, sapphire waters make it one of this Greek isle's must-see sites.

windows-spotlight-12391.jpg.title: Rebuilt Olsztyn Castle at Dusk, Olsztyn, Poland
windows-spotlight-12391.jpg.headline: A rebuilt bulwark
windows-spotlight-12391.jpg.description: A plundered ruin before its recent restoration, Bobolice Castle is one of 25 castles in the defensive network now called the Trail of the Eagle's Nests. Most are thought to have been built in the 14th century under Casimir the Great, who inherited the war-torn Kingdom of Poland and made it a prosperous power. Mostly built on high promontories and slopes, the Eagle's Nests bolstered Poland's mountainous western border against rivals like Bohemia. Bobolice did its part until the Swedes sacked it in 1657, leaving it a half-demolished husk until reconstruction began in 2004.

windows-spotlight-12395.jpg.title: Sloth mother and baby clinging to tree branch
windows-spotlight-12395.jpg.headline: Tree hugger in training
windows-spotlight-12395.jpg.description: Three-toed sloth cubs are born complete with claws and a scratchy fur coat, clinging to their mothers for about 5 months after their birth. While they nurse constantly for about the first month, they also get an early intro to adult sloths' vegetarian diet by licking leftover leaf fragments from their mother's mouth. Sounds a little gross, but this helps the cub learn which leaf varieties are safe to eat—a skill that'll serve it well for a long time to come, since wild sloths can live 30 years or more.

windows-spotlight-12398.jpg.title: Honu swimming in clear ocean water, Tunnels Beach, Kauai
windows-spotlight-12398.jpg.headline: Howdy do, honu?
windows-spotlight-12398.jpg.description: Depending who you ask and where you go, you'll hear different names for our hard-backed buddy here: Known to most English speakers as the green or black sea turtle, the species is traditionally called 'honu' here in Hawaii. With their affinity for sleeping in the sand and swimming close to shore, honu are the most commonly seen of the five sea turtle species living in the state. No matter which island you visit (our photo shows the jagged coast of Kaua'i), you're very likely to encounter these gentle reptiles on a Hawaiian vacation—but if you see one, give it plenty of personal space. It's illegal in Hawaii to touch any type of sea turtle, and keeping at least 10 feet of distance is recommended.

windows-spotlight-124.jpg.title: Cloud-filled Haleakala volcanic crater, Haleakala National Park, Maui, Hawaii
windows-spotlight-124.jpg.headline: A volcanic view
windows-spotlight-124.jpg.description: Hawaiian folklore holds that Haleakalā Crater is home to the creator of the Hawaiian Islands, Māui. It's certainly true that most of this same-named island sprang straight from here on Haleakalā: The giant shield volcano makes up about three-quarters of Maui's total area. If you're up for a brisk break from the beach, the Sliding Sands Trail offers an 11-mile scramble to Haleakalā's summit—with plenty of stunning photo ops along the way.

windows-spotlight-12400.jpg.title: Sukhothai Historical Park Dawn Reflection, Thailand
windows-spotlight-12400.jpg.headline: Dawn of a dynasty
windows-spotlight-12400.jpg.description: Before changing its name to Thailand in 1939, this Southeast Asian nation was known by outsiders as the Kingdom of Siam—and in a sense, Sukhothai is where it all started. Founded by the Khmer Empire, this ancient city was overthrown in the mid-13th century by Thai tribes led by Si Inthrathit. Rising quickly to become one of several regional Thai kingdoms known as mandalas, Sukhothai was later absorbed by more powerful neighbors. But Si Inthrathit's influence lived on in his bloodline, considered the first Siamese dynasty. Today, Sukhothai is designated as a UNESCO site, protecting its influential architecture and civic works like canals, ponds, and dams.

windows-spotlight-1241.jpg.title: Wild Goose Island, Saint Mary Lake, golden light mountains, Glacier National Park, Montana
windows-spotlight-1241.jpg.headline: Cinematic serenity
windows-spotlight-1241.jpg.description: Glacier National Park's Saint Mary Lake marks a meeting point of the Rocky Mountains and the Great Plains—with all the topographical drama that entails. Bound by soaring peaks and smooth waters, the speck of land we see in the middle of the lake is a popular place to aim a camera. The monumental vista surrounding Wild Goose Island may also be familiar to horror movie fans—it plays a prominent role in the opening credits of 'The Shining.'

windows-spotlight-12411.jpg.title: Pink Granite Boulders, Sunset, Côte de Granit Rose, Brittany, France
windows-spotlight-12411.jpg.headline: Blushing boulders
windows-spotlight-12411.jpg.description: This miles-long stretch along France's northwestern coast is defined by granite boulders and crags tracing countless small bays, inlets, and islets. Many of the area's seaside stone formations are nicknamed after their shapes: Imaginative observers say a rabbit, a shark, a turtle, a witch, and other colorful characters can be found outlined in the outcrops. But it's the slight rosy tint borne by the boulders that gives this part of Brittany its common name: Côte de Granit Rose, or Pink Granite Coast.

windows-spotlight-12414.jpg.title: Blue Bubble Nebula
windows-spotlight-12414.jpg.headline: Space blows
windows-spotlight-12414.jpg.description: Give the world champion bubble-blower all the gum ever made and they still couldn't match the mass of this seemingly inflatable space object—seen here as snapped by the Hubble Telescope. The 'lungs' that blew up the Bubble Nebula belong to the flared point of light in the sphere's upper left—a star called BD+602522, whose stellar winds force gas and dust outward in all directions, ballooning to a diameter of 6 light years or more. We hate to burst your bubble, but even stars breathe their last eventually: Astronomers think BD+602522 will go supernova in 10 to 20 million years, a cosmic cataclysm sure to make this nebula pop.
windows-spotlight-12414.jpg.copyright: © NASA, ESA, and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

windows-spotlight-12417.jpg.title: Golden Sunset Clouds Reflected on Mountain Lake
windows-spotlight-12417.jpg.headline: Light on the lake
windows-spotlight-12417.jpg.description: In this sunset shot of Herbert Lake in Alberta, Canada, lazy clouds and calm waters appear to rush past at a clip. This apparent motion blur is a side effect of the long exposure technique used to create the photo's rich lighting. By setting the camera shutter to remain open longer when the trigger is pressed, a photographer can allow more light to reach the camera's sensor. The tricky part? Moving objects will leave 'trails' that track their motion for as long as the shutter is open. Stationary objects, like the evergreens in the photo's center, will remain in crisp focus—as long as the camera remains very still, meaning most shots like this require a sturdy, stable tripod.

windows-spotlight-12418.jpg.title: Illuminated Wat Chaiwatthanaram night reflection, Ayutthaya, Thailand
windows-spotlight-12418.jpg.headline: A wat worth witnessing
windows-spotlight-12418.jpg.description: Wat Chaiwatthanaram wasn't always a place of peaceful reflection. Previously neglected (except by sneaky treasure hunters) for centuries, the wat still bears scars from cannonballs that struck it in 1767, when it doubled as a fortress. That battle put it more or less off the map until the Thai government began restoring it in 1987—just one part of a massive renovation that started in the '60s and resulted in Ayutthaya Historical Park. Covering a little more than a square mile, the park preserves the old capital city of the Ayutthaya kingdom, considered the precursor of modern Thailand.

windows-spotlight-12421.jpg.title: Blue Crystal Ice Cave
windows-spotlight-12421.jpg.headline: Crystal caves
windows-spotlight-12421.jpg.description: Ice caves occur when freezing-cold underground chambers are permeated by water, which accumulates as ice on the stone surfaces. On the other hand, what we're seeing here is a glacier cave formed within solid ice, its only stone support being the bedrock below. Tunneling under the solid ice of Switzerland's Morteratsch Glacier, this particular cave is one of several here that make popular attractions winter after winter. But a tour of the caves is never the same twice, as they melt and shift during the off-season summer months.

windows-spotlight-12423.jpg.title: A marina alight
windows-spotlight-12423.jpg.headline: A marina alight
windows-spotlight-12423.jpg.description: Less than a mile from the oceanic Singapore Strait and framed by glowing skyscrapers, Marina Bay is formed by the meeting of the Singapore, Kallang, Geylang, and Rochor rivers. That means it's full of freshwater that's much gentler on rust-prone boat hulls than the saltwater held at bay by the Marina Barrage dam. Unlike the city-state's busy port system, though, this safe harbor is only accessible from the inland side, with the dam preventing passage to and from the great, salty beyond. Surrounding the bay is Singapore's beating heart: the Downtown Core, which hosts the city-state's famous finance sector and many high-rise hotels, also acting as a mass transit hub and center of government.

windows-spotlight-12431.jpg.title: Snowy forest lake winter, Hintersee
windows-spotlight-12431.jpg.headline: A Hintersee winter scene
windows-spotlight-12431.jpg.description: Glimmering on the border of Berchtesgaden National Park is a lake that's inspired explorers and artists for centuries—regardless of the season. It's not hard to see where all the adoration comes from: Hintersee's setting, lying beneath the Reiteralm and Hochkalter mountains, is at once idyllic and breathtaking. The lake sits within Ramsau, a particularly scenic corner of Bavaria that includes the Watzmann, the highest mountain located entirely on German soil.

windows-spotlight-12434.jpg.title: Duomo di Milano and Colonnade in morning, Milan
windows-spotlight-12434.jpg.headline: Milan by morning
windows-spotlight-12434.jpg.description: Milan is one of the European Union's biggest metropolises and one of the most visited cities in the world, but it's not without its quiet moments. Lying at the center of the city, even the Piazza del Duomo is starkly empty at this early-morning hour. Looming over the soon-to-be-tourist-filled void is the Piazza's namesake, the Duomo aka Milan Cathedral. A stunning and influential work of Gothic architecture that took 6 centuries to complete, the cathedral draws over 5 million visitors each year—40,000 of which can fit at once inside its expansive interior.
windows-spotlight-12434.jpg.copyright: © Jonathan Herbert I JH Images/Moment/Getty Images

windows-spotlight-12436.jpg.title: Waterfront skyscrapers, sunset reflection, Miami
windows-spotlight-12436.jpg.headline: Miami nice
windows-spotlight-12436.jpg.description: This soothing sunset shot shows but a sliver of the continental United States' southernmost metropolis. In terms of skyscraper density, Miami punches up with the biggest megalopolises in the US, boasting the nation's third-biggest skyline after New York City and Chicago. In addition to its more than 300 high-rises, the Miami metro's marine geography demands its fair share of engineering, with lengthy road links (like the distant Rickenbacker Causeway) crossing Biscayne Bay to connect various barrier islands and keys.

windows-spotlight-12442.jpg.title: Wat Sirindhorn Wararam Phu Prao blue phosphorescence, Ubon Ratchathani Province
windows-spotlight-12442.jpg.headline: Phu Prao phosphorescence
windows-spotlight-12442.jpg.description: While the province of Ubon Ratchathani in northeast Thailand is renowned for its abundance of natural beauty, one of the more spectacular sights is a glowing tribute to human creativity. Visit Wat Sirindhorn Wararam Phu Prao (or Phu Prao Temple) during the day and you'll find a Buddhist temple combining traditional Thai and Lao architecture, as well as breathtaking views from its hilltop perch above the Mekong River. Stick around after sunset for the lightshow: Phosphorescent paint, after absorbing the day's sunshine, radiates blue and green glows in swirling designs. On the ground are spirals, vines, and floral motifs, and on the side of the temple itself is the central artwork—a large and lustrous Tree of Life.

windows-spotlight-12448.jpg.title: Gypsum sand dunes, White Sands National Park, New Mexico
windows-spotlight-12448.jpg.headline: Sea of snow?
windows-spotlight-12448.jpg.description: At a quick glance, you might mistake these southern New Mexico dunes for massive snowdrifts. Although they do make for great sledding, the tiny crystals that form White Sands National Park are not ice but gypsum, a soft mineral often used in plaster and chalk. The pearly sands compose part of the largest gypsum field in the world, at 176,000 acres and more than 4 billion tons of sand. Extensive as it is, this sea of alabaster covers just a fraction of the Tularosa Basin, a vast desert valley that's larger than some US states at roughly 6,500 square miles.

windows-spotlight-12454.jpg.title: Mount Ngauruhoe movie fame volcano sunset, Tongariro National Park, New Zealand
windows-spotlight-12454.jpg.headline: Mount of movie fame
windows-spotlight-12454.jpg.description: The fictional, fuming Mount Doom was portrayed by two different New Zealand peaks in the 'Lord of the Rings' movies, and here we see one of them: a sun-soaked Mount Ngauruhoe. With roughly 70 eruptions since recordkeeping began, Ngauruhoe is the most active of at least a dozen cones making up the stratovolcano complex called Tongariro. The last of its blasts happened back in 1977, making this the longest recorded period of dormancy in its 2,500-year existence—but its fellow Mount Doom stand-in, nearby Mount Ruapehu, has remained active well into the 21st century.

windows-spotlight-12458.jpg.title: Snow-covered alpine hairpin road, light trails
windows-spotlight-12458.jpg.headline: An alpine hairpin
windows-spotlight-12458.jpg.description: Like this headlight-streaked stretch, most mountain roads are arranged in switchbacks, zigzagging back and forth upslope rather than leading straight to the summit. The snaking shape has two advantages: First, it keeps grades shallow enough for a typical car to climb, and second, a straight-line road would create an easy path for snow melt and other erosive forces, leading to flooding and landslides. Of course, while they're clearly the safest approach to road design on steep surfaces, switchback routes inevitably involve a little white-knuckling while navigating hairpin turns like this doozy in the Italian Alps.

windows-spotlight-12459.jpg.title: Melting blue glacier cave
windows-spotlight-12459.jpg.headline: A melting marvel
windows-spotlight-12459.jpg.description: Venture past a certain elevation and it seems that the mighty Alps are a land of everlasting winter, but don't take the chill for granted. We're peering out from the inside of an Alpine glacier cave as a cross-country skier surveys its open mouth—a portal to a frozen fantasy world that's slowly disappearing. Since its position was first recorded more than a century and a half ago, this massive patch of ice—northern Italy's Forni Glacier—has retreated about 2 miles, losing about half its volume. Unfortunately, this isn't a unique predicament among Alpine glaciers: Virtually all are in retreat, and without interventions to slow climate change, as much as two-thirds of the Alps' ice mass is projected to melt by 2100.

windows-spotlight-12461.jpg.title: Colorful Dahlia Blooms, Flower Farm, Portland, Oregon, USA
windows-spotlight-12461.jpg.headline: A petaled panoply
windows-spotlight-12461.jpg.description: This grab bag of buds and blooms showcases just a smidgeon of the possibilities presented by this flexible flower genus. More than 40 species of dahlia are officially recognized, and through hybridization and selective breeding, hundreds of colors and shapes can be realized in their proliferous petals. The starburst quality of their blossoms is reflected in their family name: Asteraceae, a vast classification that encompasses sunflowers, daisies, mums, and many more. Native to Mexico, dahlias can thrive just about anywhere frost is rare—the floral rainbow in our photo is from a large farm near Portland, Oregon.

windows-spotlight-12462.jpg.title: Athabasca River, Snow-capped Mountain, Evergreen Forest, Jasper National Park, Canadian Rockies
windows-spotlight-12462.jpg.headline: Athabasca flow
windows-spotlight-12462.jpg.description: One of the most important rivers in Alberta, the glacier-fed Athabasca rises in the Columbia Icefield here in Jasper National Park. It snakes amid the park's many peaks—including Mount Kerkeslin, looming large in our photo—before tumbling over Athabasca Falls just a stone's throw from this pebble-strewn spot. The river's cross-province course, flowing generally northeast, covers 765 miles before emptying into Lake Athabasca, the 8th-largest of Canada's estimated 2 million lakes.

windows-spotlight-12466.jpg.title: Upsala Glacier, Snow-capped Mountains, Glacial Lake, Los Glaciares National Park, Patagonia, Argentina
windows-spotlight-12466.jpg.headline: A crumbling giant
windows-spotlight-12466.jpg.description: This sweeping tendril of frosty blue looks impossibly large on its own, but it's just one exit glacier of the enormous Northern Patagonian Ice Field—one of the world's biggest masses of ice. At the point where it meets San Rafael Lake, huge icebergs often crumble off the glacier's edge into the tidal waters below, which connect to the Pacific Ocean via a series of channels and fjords. The thunderous spectacle is popular with tourists, who flock to cruise boats and kayak tours for a closer look at the calving action.

windows-spotlight-12475.jpg.title: Five Finger Islands Lighthouse, snow-capped mountains, Frederick Sound, Alaska
windows-spotlight-12475.jpg.headline: Prospectors' passage
windows-spotlight-12475.jpg.description: Though built in 1906, some years after the Klondike Gold Rush, the Eldred Rock Lighthouse marks one of the most important waterways used by prospectors of that period. Leading straight to boomtowns like Skagway and Dyea, and connected to the capital Juneau via the Gastineau Channel, the 90-mile fjord called Lynn Canal was the go-to route for fortune seekers in the fateful years of 1896-99. Prospect in these parts today and you're facing even longer odds than those grizzled gold diggers—but a mother lode of great views is a sure thing on this passage plied by numerous cruise lines as well as the Alaska Marine Highway.

windows-spotlight-12481.jpg.title: Cerulean Skaftafell Ice Cave, Iceland
windows-spotlight-12481.jpg.headline: A cerulean cavern
windows-spotlight-12481.jpg.description: Hidden just outside Juneau, Alaska, the Mendenhall Glacier feels almost unreal, inside and out. Step into one of its rare blue caves, and the world turns quiet and luminous, with light filtering through centuries-old compacted ice. The glacier stretches about 13 miles from the Juneau Icefield, slowly flowing toward the valley below and reshaping itself year by year. While reaching the caves has become increasingly rare and unpredictable, the glacier remains closely studied, offering scientists a visible record of environmental change.

windows-spotlight-12487.jpg.title: Rainbow Bridge National Monument, Utah
windows-spotlight-12487.jpg.headline: Staircase to heaven
windows-spotlight-12487.jpg.description: The Grand Staircase–Escalante National Monument contains an expanse of stunning rock formations in southern Utah. The monument, established in 1996, spans more than 2,900 square miles and is one of several national parks and reserves located along the Grand Staircase. The layers of sediment, stacked like stair steps, date back as far as 600 million years. Many of these layers include fossils of long-extinct creatures, and the area is a hotspot for paleontologists: In 2002, a gryposaurus fossil, roughly 75 million years old, was found near the monument's Arizona border.

windows-spotlight-12488.jpg.title: Stone Church, Sunken Village Remnant, Lac du Chevril, French Alps
windows-spotlight-12488.jpg.headline: A sunken town's remnant
windows-spotlight-12488.jpg.description: Above the body of water that engulfed its predecessors, a humble chapel stands watch in the hills. Despite its weathered look, Roselend Chapel has only stood here since Roselend Dam (seen as just a sliver on the right edge of our photo) was completed in the early 1960s. As the basin below filled with water, the abandoned French village of Roselend—including its Romanesque chapel dating to the 12th century—was fully submerged. This backstory is told in brief by the chapel's dual bells: The one on the right is an original from the now-sunken chapel, while the shiny one on the left was cast in 2011 (replacing a second original that was stolen in the 1980s).

windows-spotlight-12490.jpg.title: Jade Geothermal Crater Lakes, Tongariro National Park, New Zealand
windows-spotlight-12490.jpg.headline: Craters of jade
windows-spotlight-12490.jpg.description: Whether rendered in English or Māori, the name of these teal-tinted lakes hints at a verdant precious stone. On most maps they're called the Emerald Lakes, while the older name Ngā Rotopounamu references pounamu—a word for nephrite jade and similar hard, green stones found in other parts of New Zealand. It's not just the names here that bear a geological air: Set in the contours of Tongariro National Park—the country's oldest—the lakes are formed from extinct volcanic craters and surrounded by geothermal activity.

windows-spotlight-12496.jpg.title: Sunrise Mountain Lake Ripple
windows-spotlight-12496.jpg.headline: Ripple in still water
windows-spotlight-12496.jpg.description: In fancy science talk, ripples are known as capillary waves, and they're just one of many focuses in the expansive field of fluid dynamics. They're a delicate thing: If the wavelength of a ripple gets too big, it begins seeing substantial effects from gravity, disturbing the ripple's symmetry. Even undisturbed, a ripple is never really a perfect circle—as we see in this shot of Plansee, a crystal-clear alpine lake in Austria, where short, subtle waves from a gentle wind give our ripple a slightly shuddering shape.

windows-spotlight-12503.jpg.title: Forbidden City Corner Tower sunset, Beijing
windows-spotlight-12503.jpg.headline: Domicile of dynasties
windows-spotlight-12503.jpg.description: We're looking at a quiet corner of one of the world's most visited tourist destinations—the Forbidden City in Beijing. This former imperial palace in China's capital city receives over 16 million visitors every year, making it the most visited UNESCO World Heritage Site. Built in the 15th century, the Forbidden City was home to 24 emperors, including the last emperor of China, who abdicated in 1912. The vast palace complex was the seat of power for these emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties, and within the city there are hundreds of buildings and nearly 10,000 rooms, housing a remarkable collection of art and artifacts.

windows-spotlight-12509.jpg.title: Snow-capped, Cloud-crowned Crater, Lenticular Clouds, Sunset
windows-spotlight-12509.jpg.headline: A cloud-crowned crater
windows-spotlight-12509.jpg.description: Known for its symmetry and smooth snowcap, the volcanic cone called Parinacota is seen beneath billowy lenticular clouds in this soft-glow shot. Along with its neighbor peak Pomerape, Parinacota is part of the short Nevados de Payachatas chain marking the border of Bolivia and Chile. Volcanoes abound here in the Andes, numbering around 150 and divided into four distinct zones. Along with the Central Volcanic Zone that includes Parinacota, the Northern Zone covers the volcanoes of Ecuador and Colombia, and the Southern and Austral Zones straddle the long, squiggly border of Chile and Argentina.

windows-spotlight-1251.jpg.title: Flock of Sandhill Cranes flying, Rio Grande
windows-spotlight-1251.jpg.headline: Rest stop on the Rio
windows-spotlight-1251.jpg.description: Rich rows of cottonwoods shade the marshy banks of the Rio Grande at this highway-side wilderness about an hour south of Albuquerque. Known as the Bosque del Apache, the 57,000-acre protected area is an oasis for migrating birds, especially sandhill cranes such as these. They're among tens of thousands of waterfowl that vacation here beginning in the fall, as leaves take on the signature ochres of a New Mexico autumn.

windows-spotlight-12511.jpg.title: Sunshine Skyway Bridge illuminated dusk, Tampa Bay, Florida
windows-spotlight-12511.jpg.headline: One good bridge deserves…
windows-spotlight-12511.jpg.description: This bridge's everyday name implies the existence of another—the Penang Second Bridge shown here aglow at twilight is indeed the younger of two major bridges serving Penang Island. One category where it's not second  is length, stretching about 15 miles including 10 over open water. That's almost 7 miles longer than the original Penang Bridge, making the Second Bridge the longest span in Malaysia. And it carries a lengthy official name to match: the Sultan Abdul Halim Muadzam Shah Bridge.

windows-spotlight-12512.jpg.title: Fiery Sunset Glow on Great Divide Peaks and Alpine River
windows-spotlight-12512.jpg.headline: Glow over the Great Divide
windows-spotlight-12512.jpg.description: In this stretch of the Canadian Rockies where two provinces straddle the Great Divide, the winding dotted line on the map marks many remarkable peaks. These include Mount Assiniboine—the Matterhorn-esque mount that's the tallest in the region and this provincial park's namesake—and the raggedy massif known as the Towers, showcased in this wide-angle shot. The Towers' several summits mark British Columbia's border with neighbor province Alberta, though the land just past the peaks is managed by the Canadian government as Banff National Park.

windows-spotlight-12513.jpg.title: Turquoise Lake and Snow-Capped Mountains, Central Asian Steppe
windows-spotlight-12513.jpg.headline: Get your steppes in
windows-spotlight-12513.jpg.description: Twice the size of Texas but with less than an eighth of its population, Mongolia is the world's most sparsely populated country. Mostly defined by the wide, flat steppes that top the Mongolian Plateau, its 604,000 square miles are home to just 3.5 million people, about half of whom live in the capital city Ulaanbaatar. Here in Bayan-Ölgii, the westernmost of Mongolia's 21 aimags, we're about as far from the capital as you can get while remaining in the country. Mongolia, China, Russia, and Kazakhstan form a near-quadripoint in this region where the Altai Mountains rise and chilly, clear mountain lakes—like Tolbo Lake here—fill pockets between peaks and foothills.

windows-spotlight-12515.jpg.title: Orange gas pillars and stars in Lobster Nebula
windows-spotlight-12515.jpg.headline: Stars in a pinch
windows-spotlight-12515.jpg.description: From a wider perspective, the Lobster Nebula indeed looks like an astronomically-sized arthropod claw, but a zoomed-up view of this space crustacean reveals complexity we've only begun to comprehend. The numberless twinkles in our image belong to newborn stars of the open cluster Pismis 24, a stellar nursery hosting some of the heaviest and highest-intensity stars we know of. Pismis 24-1, seen here at low center, is the most massive star in the cluster. Once considered the largest known star, it was later found to be multiple stars—each still dozens of times bigger and brighter than the sun.
windows-spotlight-12515.jpg.copyright: © NASA, ESA, CSA, and STScI Image Processing: M. Garcia Marin, A. Pagan (STScI)

windows-spotlight-12516.jpg.title: Milky Way galaxy framed by Double Arch, Arches National Park, Utah
windows-spotlight-12516.jpg.headline: 2,000 arches, infinite sky
windows-spotlight-12516.jpg.description: Like giants on guard, scattered stone formations stand in silhouette as darkness falls on Arches National Park. Nary a streetlight dulls the piercing stars in this remote region of Utah, where the mountain-biking hotspot of Moab—population about 5,000—is the closest thing to a metropolis. Under clear conditions, nightfall reveals the Milky Way in its full, sky-spanning arc, appearing especially sharp when caught on camera. The lucky photographer behind today's shot caught this galactic scene as seen through one of the twin 'windows' of Double Arch—one of the park's more than 2,000 natural arches.

windows-spotlight-12517.jpg.title: Sandstone hoodoos under blue sky, Goblin Valley State Park, Utah
windows-spotlight-12517.jpg.headline: Get a gander at the goblins
windows-spotlight-12517.jpg.description: Arches, Canyonlands, Zion—these famous names conjure scenes of monumental rock formations and endless desert vistas. But those top-billed Utah destinations aren't the only 'rock stars' around. In fact, there's a lesser-known (read: less crowded) park chock-full of some of the most breathtaking geologic formations in the American Southwest. Within Goblin Valley State Park is one of the highest concentrations of hoodoos on Earth. Around here, hoodoos are known as goblins, and they're the stars of this park, where erosion has worked its natural magic on soft Entrada sandstone over millions of years.

windows-spotlight-12520.jpg.title: Lakeside village of Hallstatt, Austria
windows-spotlight-12520.jpg.headline: Heavenly Hallstatt
windows-spotlight-12520.jpg.description: This area of pristine alpine lakes and sawtooth peaks in Upper Austria is known as the Salzkammergut or 'Estate of The Salt Chamber.' For centuries, salt was mined—and in some cases still is—from caves within the impressive limestone peaks of the Dachstein massif. Dotted throughout the range are large lakes, some undeveloped, but most hosting small villages on portions of their shores. Here we see the village of Hallstatt on the lake named after it, Hallstätter See—a place of such renowned beauty that overtourism is a mounting concern.

windows-spotlight-12521.jpg.title: Los Muertos Pier and anchored boats under red evening sky, Puerto Vallarta, Mexico
windows-spotlight-12521.jpg.headline: Of piers and pangas
windows-spotlight-12521.jpg.description: Opened in 2013, the sleek, stylish Los Muertos Pier serves Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, as the flashier sequel to two much simpler predecessors. The first was a ramshackle wooden structure built to ferry camera equipment for the 1964 film 'The Night of the Iguana,' later replaced by a simple, sturdy concrete outcrop. The latest pier is a tourist attraction in itself, but it's also a gateway to further fun in the sun: Small skiffs known as pangas flock to and from the lower dock, offering passage directly from the pier to many of the region's beaches. Once the bustle dies down in the evening, the fleet can be seen anchored near the pier, typically framed by one of the city's signature sunsets.

windows-spotlight-12522.jpg.title: Granite coastal boulders and sailboat on Indian Ocean, Praslin, Seychelles
windows-spotlight-12522.jpg.headline: Haze on the waves
windows-spotlight-12522.jpg.description: Home to barely over 100,000 people across 115 small islands, Seychelles is considered the smallest African country by both population and area. About 800 miles of Indian Ocean waves separate Seychelles from the second-largest continent, and the island group's granite bedrock (seen here in the form of protruding coastal boulders) is unusual in a place this far from any mainland—long cited as evidence for continental drift. These particular rocks peek through ocean mists along the coast of Praslin, the country's second-largest island after the main one, Mahé.

windows-spotlight-12523.jpg.title: Angkor Wat, Cambodia
windows-spotlight-12523.jpg.headline: Modeled on a mountain
windows-spotlight-12523.jpg.description: Construction on Angkor Wat began in the early 12th century, originally intended as a temple dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu. But by the dawn of the 13th century, it had been redefined as a Buddhist holy site. Symbols, artwork, and other details represent both faiths. Angkor Wat and the nearby city of Siem Reap are among Cambodia's most popular destinations. The temple's quincunx of towers represents the mythic Mount Meru. The idea of the massive mountain appears in both Hindu and Buddhist texts, and it  is described as the center of the cosmos.

windows-spotlight-12526.jpg.title: Hot air balloons, Maasai Mara reserve
windows-spotlight-12526.jpg.headline: One jeep if by land…
windows-spotlight-12526.jpg.description: The choice between 4x4 vehicle and hot-air balloon is only one dilemma facing folks seeking adventure on the savanna. Here's another: Kenya or Tanzania? While much of the unique landscape that hosts the Great Migration—including Serengeti National Park—lies within Tanzania, the similarly safari-suited Maasai Mara reserve pictured here lies just across the Kenyan border. Giraffes, hyenas, bush elephants, and the African big cat trinity—lions, leopards, and cheetahs—make up just a portion of the plentiful wildlife you might spot here from land or air.

windows-spotlight-12527.jpg.title: Tree-topped sea stack, Second Beach
windows-spotlight-12527.jpg.headline: Shipwreck vs. shoelaces
windows-spotlight-12527.jpg.description: The treacherous coastal waters of northwestern Washington are marked by many sea stacks, including this tree-topped ridge resembling the bow of a beached boat. Here on Second Beach, it's an apt marker: In the midst of World War II, this regionally popular recreation spot was the site of a daring, MacGyver-esque rescue. In 1943, when a Russian freighter wrecked off Teahwhit Head at the beach's southern edge, the United States Coast Guard scrambled through dense forest to reach the survivors. Tossing the crew a string of tethered shoelaces from the cliffs above, they retrieved a heavier rope from the ship and anchored it to dry land, pulling more than 50 sailors to safety over churning seas.

windows-spotlight-12529.jpg.title: Lac Blanc, Chamonix region
windows-spotlight-12529.jpg.headline: Site of a snowy showdown
windows-spotlight-12529.jpg.description: Lac Blanc shimmers beneath the peaks of the Alps in France's spectacularly scenic Chamonix region. The lakeshore and surrounding hills are popular hiking spots in summer. But it's the chilly season that's truly synonymous with Chamonix: The area hosted the first Winter Olympics way back in 1924. Then branded as 'International Winter Sports Week,' the 10-day event drew athletes from only 16 countries, but set the stage for winter sports to scale up and spread across the globe. As of the 2026 games, the participating country count is up to a healthy 93.

windows-spotlight-12531.jpg.title: Candy-stripe hot air balloon, Courchevel
windows-spotlight-12531.jpg.headline: Aloft in the Alps
windows-spotlight-12531.jpg.description: This shot and its candy-stripe subject hover over Courchevel, an Alpine destination that's part of Les Trois Vallées, or the Three Valleys—the largest interlinked ski area in the world. If you're not the type to launch off ski jumps or strap yourself to a paraglider, the humble hot air balloon offers a chance to catch air in a chiller fashion. In this peak-strewn part of France, even getting airborne might not take you above the highest land elevations—but height isn't the point so much as the 360-degree view of this winter wonderland.

windows-spotlight-12535.jpg.title: Harbor Seals
windows-spotlight-12535.jpg.headline: Going with the floe
windows-spotlight-12535.jpg.description: In most circumstances, harbor seals spend about half their time in the water and half hauled out on shore, whether it be on a beach or mudflat, a sunny stone slab, or an ice floe. The mama and pup in our photo need a little extra downtime for the time being: While able to swim from birth, the little one needs to conserve its limited energy until it's able to blubber up a bit. On the other flipper, mama is hauled out not just to protect her pup but also for hygienic purposes. Harbor seals molt shortly after breeding, and since new hair growth requires blood flow close to the skin, spending time in less frigid temps outside the water helps the seal's spiffy fur coat fill out faster.

windows-spotlight-12537.jpg.title: Wetland, Ōtūwharekai
windows-spotlight-12537.jpg.headline: A trailside wetland
windows-spotlight-12537.jpg.description: Though small and shallow, the several lakes that dot this patch of Canterbury land share an outsized cultural cachet. Named the Māori Lakes after New Zealand's indigenous peoples, this grouping of South Island sloughs doesn't get any deeper than 3 feet, making for a wetland-like environment frequented by various waterfowl. The Ngāi Tahu—the principal Māori tribe on the South Island—refer to the lake region as Ōtūwharekai, holding it in high importance as an ancient food-gathering stop on routes between the island's east and west coasts.

windows-spotlight-1254.jpg.title: Walls of China Rock Formations Sunset, Mungo National Park
windows-spotlight-1254.jpg.headline: Arid and ancient
windows-spotlight-1254.jpg.description: While it's the most populous state in Australia, New South Wales stretches into some sparse territory. Here at Mungo National Park, the parched earth stands in sharp contrast to the state capital's green shores 500 miles east. Mungo is one of the Willandra Lakes, which despite their name are usually devoid of water: Lake Mungo and the 16 neighboring beds have been dry for roughly 18,000 years. A meeting site for Aboriginal Australian nations before colonists seized it, the area was home in even earlier times to Mungo Man and Mungo Lady—thought to be the country's oldest unearthed human remains.

windows-spotlight-12541.jpg.title: Tropical beach, Banana Beach
windows-spotlight-12541.jpg.headline: Relatively paradise
windows-spotlight-12541.jpg.description: Lying in the Gulf of Guinea off the west coast of Africa is the island nation of São Tomé and Príncipe, made up of two main islands and a scattering of roughly a dozen other smaller islands. Our aerial image centers on Banana Beach, a popular destination on Príncipe, the smaller of the two main islands. Príncipe isn't just scenic, it's important in science history: During the total solar eclipse in 1919, astronomer Arthur Stanley Eddington observed the event from the island, verifying Albert Einstein's theory of relativity by photographing the gravitational deflection of starlight.

windows-spotlight-12543.jpg.title: Cracked Ice, Lake Khövsgöl
windows-spotlight-12543.jpg.headline: Frozen fractures
windows-spotlight-12543.jpg.description: It's recommended that ice be at least 4 inches thick for an average-size person to walk on it. In places like northern Mongolia, where winter temps regularly dip deep below zero, ice thickness tends to skate right by that minimum requirement—but hairline cracks may still form even in sturdy ice, as shown in this close-up of Lake Khövsgöl's frozen surface. The lake is Mongolia's largest by volume, and due to its freshwater composition, it freezes much more readily than the nation's numerous saline lakes.

windows-spotlight-12548.jpg.title: Rocky sea stacks, Harris Beach State Park
windows-spotlight-12548.jpg.headline: A hidden Northwest gem
windows-spotlight-12548.jpg.description: In the far southern stretches of Oregon is a state park that's a microcosm of what makes this region's coastline so special: a wide expanse of soft sand and rocky tide pools, plenty of thriving wildlife, and sea stacks lining the surf with Sitka spruce towering over the bluffs. Bonus? Harris Beach State Park isn't typically crowded like the more heavily touristed parts of the coastline up north. There's an off-the-beaten-path vibe about the place, but it's not inaccessible. Modern facilities are available, and campers reserve spots for RVs, tents, and even yurts well in advance.

windows-spotlight-12550.jpg.title: Tea Plantations, Cameron Highlands
windows-spotlight-12550.jpg.headline: High tea
windows-spotlight-12550.jpg.description: Named for William Cameron, a geologist who first mapped the area for Britain in 1885, the Cameron Highlands are renowned for their mild climate. This wouldn't be so noteworthy except that the lush landscape is part of Malaysia, a country whose lower elevations often swelter in tropical heat. The air here is ideal for both the expansive tea plantations carpeting the rolling landscape, and for an extensive tourist trade that keeps this corner of fantastically scenic Pahang state buzzing. Fortify yourself with a few cups of tea before you head out for other Cameron Highlands attractions: rainforest hikes, temple tours, historic townships, and world-class strawberry farms.

windows-spotlight-12551.jpg.title: Sea stacks, Harris Beach State Park
windows-spotlight-12551.jpg.headline: A hidden Northwest gem
windows-spotlight-12551.jpg.description: In the far southern stretches of Oregon is a state park that's a microcosm of what makes this region's coastline so special: a wide expanse of soft sand and rocky tide pools, plenty of thriving wildlife, and sea stacks lining the surf with Sitka spruce towering over the bluffs. Modern facilities are available, and campers reserve spots for RVs, tents, and even yurts well in advance.

windows-spotlight-12552.jpg.title: Night cityscape, Kuala Lumpur
windows-spotlight-12552.jpg.headline: From super-tiny to supertall
windows-spotlight-12552.jpg.description: Nested in a valley surrounded by deep rainforest, Kuala Lumpur's dense cityscape only sprang up in the last century or so. Early photographs of the location, dating to the late 1800s, reveal a modest town of thatched attap dwellings, along with a few British colonial buildings in Mughal and Moorish styles. But since Malaysia gained independence in 1957, the capital has earned fame for the high-rising stars of this sparkling shot: its skyscrapers, which number in the hundreds and include supertall structures like Petronas Towers and Merdeka 118.

windows-spotlight-12556.jpg.title: Tea plantation, Cameron Highlands
windows-spotlight-12556.jpg.headline: High tea
windows-spotlight-12556.jpg.description: Named for William Cameron, a geologist who first mapped the area for Britain in 1885, the Cameron Highlands are renowned for their mild climate. This wouldn't be so noteworthy except that the lush landscape is part of Malaysia, a country whose lower elevations often swelter in tropical heat. The air here is ideal for both the expansive tea plantations carpeting the rolling landscape, and for an extensive tourist trade that keeps this corner of fantastically scenic Pahang state buzzing. Fortify yourself with a few cups of tea before you head out for other Cameron Highlands attractions: rainforest hikes, temple tours, historic townships, and world-class strawberry farms.

windows-spotlight-12559.jpg.title: Thatched bungalows, Ko Phayam
windows-spotlight-12559.jpg.headline: Kayaking Ko Phayam
windows-spotlight-12559.jpg.description: Consisting of an isthmus flanked by hundreds of small islands, southern Thailand might be best known internationally for its rowdy all-night beach raves. If you prefer less in the way of blinding lights and bumping basslines, turn your gaze about 120 miles north of Phuket as the crow flies and you'll find the hidden Thai paradise of Ko Phayam. Though its green shores and sandy beaches are dotted with resorts (like this one offering rustic thatched-roof bungalows and a mangrove-lined channel for kayaking), it's still far less developed than Ko Pha-ngan, Ko Samui, and other destination isles in the region.

windows-spotlight-12561.jpg.title: Bare tree, Ribblesdale
windows-spotlight-12561.jpg.headline: A dale in the dark
windows-spotlight-12561.jpg.description: More than two dozen named valleys, or dales, make up the sleepy swath of northern England known as the Yorkshire Dales (seen here beneath a rather rare aurora). Some of their names are familiar from other contexts, like Airedale for its large, scruffy terriers and Wensleydale for its mild cheese. Others lean toward the literal, like Silverdale for its silvery-gray birch woods and Deepdale for its, well, depth. This somewhat spooky scene comes to us from Ribblesdale—named for the River Ribble, which flows 75 miles from the nearby Ribblehead Viaduct to the Irish Sea. Curious about the term 'Ribble'? Its origin is lost to history—but some linguists peg it to the Old English 'ripel' for rip, perhaps for the long rift it tears through the landscape.

windows-spotlight-12566.jpg.title: Wat Tham Khao Prang, Thailand
windows-spotlight-12566.jpg.headline: A chrome-topped temple
windows-spotlight-12566.jpg.description: About 67 million Buddhists call Thailand home—more than 90% of the country's population. Buddhism has been present in Southeast Asia for at least two millennia, building a vast architectural legacy from ancient to modern. Wat Tham Khao Prang, completed in the late 1990s, lacks the rough, intricate sandstone carvings typical of older Thai temples, instead featuring clean lines and polished metal. The temple's designers didn't skimp on the iconography, though: A massive, chalk-white Buddha statue also graces the grounds.

windows-spotlight-12567.jpg.title: Red cable car, Jasper
windows-spotlight-12567.jpg.headline: Alberta altitude
windows-spotlight-12567.jpg.description: From March to October, the Jasper SkyTram takes visitors from lowlands outside the town of Jasper to a 7,500-foot-high station near the top of The Whistlers, an imposing mountain that forms a familiar backdrop to the town. The peak's oddly pluralized name refers to the noise made by a multitude that populates these slopes: hoary marmots. You can count on hearing this Rocky Mountain rodents' shrill serenade if you choose to continue after your excursion on Canada's highest cable car—a handy hiking trail leads from the SkyTram's stopping point to the summit, which stands about 600 feet higher in elevation.

windows-spotlight-1257.jpg.title: Green golden terraced fields
windows-spotlight-1257.jpg.headline: Two-tone terraces
windows-spotlight-1257.jpg.description: The disparity in tint between these stair-stepped rice fields is the difference between young and old. Recently planted green grasses, which won't bear mature rice grains for a few months, contrast with the yellow crop that's fast approaching its appointment with the sickle. Although most of Vietnam's rice production occurs in the low, flat Mekong Delta, more than a thousand acres of rice terraces rise in this pocket of northern Vietnam. Ingenious irrigation networks designed by local Hmong people keep the paddies good and soaked until harvest time, even here at 3,200 feet above sea level.

windows-spotlight-12570.jpg.title: Moonscape, Hanksville
windows-spotlight-12570.jpg.headline: Over the 'moon'
windows-spotlight-12570.jpg.description: This patch of rugged land named for its resemblance to the lunar surface is certainly more accessible than the moon—but getting here is still no moonwalk. Though the Moonscape Overlook lies just a few miles outside the town of Hanksville, Utah, it's a bumpy journey by offroad vehicle to get a firsthand gander at this otherworldly environment. But once you've made the trip to this 'moon,' feel free to stay awhile: Administered by the Bureau of Land Management, this area as well as nearby Factory Butte allow free dispersed camping—just make sure to leave no trace on this delicate desert.

windows-spotlight-12573.jpg.title: Cherry blossoms, Kyushu
windows-spotlight-12573.jpg.headline: Sakura season
windows-spotlight-12573.jpg.description: In springtime each year, people across Japan observe hanami—the treasured tradition of getting outdoors to view nature's breathtaking annual display of cherry blossoms. Japanese cherry trees, known as sakura, reach full bloom in March in the country's south, starting here on the southerly island of Kyushu. Blooms progress northward throughout March and April, passing through Greater Tokyo and ending with the late-thawing northern island of Hokkaido.

windows-spotlight-12574.jpg.title: Contoured granite boulder, Anse Source d'Argent
windows-spotlight-12574.jpg.headline: Boulder on the beach
windows-spotlight-12574.jpg.description: Cutting a staggered stegosaurus-spine shape against blue skies, this streaky stone hulk is one of many on this Seychelles shore. The boulder-bound beach of Anse Source d'Argent—located on the granitic isle of La Digue—has long been a favorite of photographers, who are drawn to its contoured, dark granite boulders, pristine white sand, and turquoise-colored water. Beachcombers and sun worshippers also flock to the Seychelles because of the consistently great weather—daily high temperatures almost always stay within a comfortable range between 75 and 90 degrees Fahrenheit year-round.

windows-spotlight-12581.jpg.title: Mountains, Fuerteventura
windows-spotlight-12581.jpg.headline: Macaronesia mist
windows-spotlight-12581.jpg.description: Though at 2,648 feet it's not breaking any height records, you'll find no better place for a panoramic picture here on Fuerteventura. Pico de la Zarza is the highest point on this laid-back and tourist-friendly isle, the second-largest of the Canary Islands and all of Macaronesia—a sprawling series of archipelagos that also includes the Azores, Madeira, and Cape Verde. Chasing big views like this? Make sure to add Tenerife to your itinerary: Just a short-hop flight away, the largest and most populous of the Canaries is also home to Mount Teide, the highest point among all Atlantic islands at 12,188 feet.

windows-spotlight-12585.jpg.title: Raudasandur, Iceland
windows-spotlight-12585.jpg.headline: A study in…scallops?
windows-spotlight-12585.jpg.description: Raudasandur is named for the slightly scarlet tint of its sands, as seen in this wide shot of the 6-mile beach. The name translates to 'red sand' in the local tongue—Icelandic, surprisingly enough given the beachy scenery. While it's the rosy hues that made their way into the name, Raudasandur actually displays a variety of colors throughout the day. The effect is due to a key ingredient in the sand: tiny bits of iridescent scallop shell, which reflect different colors depending on how the sunlight catches them.

windows-spotlight-12589.jpg.title: Milan Cathedral, Milan
windows-spotlight-12589.jpg.headline: The Duomo at dusk
windows-spotlight-12589.jpg.description: Milan Cathedral took more than 600 years to build, and as this dusky shot of Italy's second-biggest city shows, construction work never truly ends. The 21st century has been a time of major restoration for both the interior and—with the assistance of copious scaffolding—the exterior of the Duomo, as it's dearly known by Milan residents. Much of the renovation work has been funded by donations, including a program that allowed locals and businesses (and even enamored tourists) to 'adopt' one of the cathedral's 135 spires.

windows-spotlight-1259.jpg.title: Paraglider, Lake Garda, Mountain Range, Sunset, Italy
windows-spotlight-1259.jpg.headline: Go with the gusts
windows-spotlight-1259.jpg.description: Our paragliding pal here is taking advantage of the many winds that zigzag above Lake Garda, the largest lake in Italy. The steep surroundings give rise to so many winds, in fact, that many of these gales have names. Two are especially important to the local gliding and sailing scenes: the Ora and the Pelèr. On most summer mornings, the vigorous Pelèr blows south until around noon, when the Ora picks up and heads back north. Together, the twin winds create a sailor's superhighway at the narrow northern end of the lake.

windows-spotlight-12592.jpg.title: Illuminated mountain town, Bormio
windows-spotlight-12592.jpg.headline: Spa in the Alps
windows-spotlight-12592.jpg.description: Bormio is a mountain town in northern Italy's Lombardy region, nestled in the Alps near the Stelvio Pass. Bormio is known for its natural hot springs that have been documented since Roman times. Historic bathhouses, such as the Bagni Vecchi, show how thermal waters supported health, social life, and resilience during harsh winters. Today, the town is part of Stelvio National Park, where its history, landscape, and culture continue to be preserved.

windows-spotlight-12593.jpg.title: Hoodoos, Ah-Shi-Sle-Pah Wilderness
windows-spotlight-12593.jpg.headline: Stuff of dreams
windows-spotlight-12593.jpg.description: Covering a sizeable chunk of New Mexico and stretching into each of the Four Corners states, the San Juan Basin is host to both the stunning geology of the present and incredible glimpses into the past. Here we see a slice of the Ah-Shi-Sle-Pah Wilderness known as the Valley of Dreams for its somewhat hallucinatory-looking hoodoos, similar to the strange forms in nearby Bisti/De-Na-Zin. The vast high desert basin has much to offer paleontologists and archaeologists alike: Here in Ah-Shi-Sle-Pah, prehistoric fossils (including a noted species of ankylosaurus named for the spot) have been unearthed, and nearby Chaco Canyon is a well-preserved window into the Pueblo culture that thrived in this region as early as the year 900.

windows-spotlight-12595.jpg.title: Ceahlău, Romania
windows-spotlight-12595.jpg.headline: Lofty legends
windows-spotlight-12595.jpg.description: The Carpathian Mountains cover about a quarter of Romania's land area, cutting a huge horseshoe through the country's center. Though our panoramic perch isn't the range's highest summit (that'd be the 8,350-foot Moldoveanu Peak), this massif known as Ceahlău might be the stuff of more legends, from tales of gods and devils to hyped-up histories of Roman conquest. Maybe the most famous involves a rock called Panagia—said to have been a beautiful peasant girl who climbed Ceahlău to court the sun itself, eventually turning to stone while waiting for her lover to emerge from the clouds.

windows-spotlight-12596.jpg.title: Cerro Torre reflected in glacial lake, Patagonia, Argentina
windows-spotlight-12596.jpg.headline: Climber's conundrum
windows-spotlight-12596.jpg.description: Peering past floating glacial icebergs and rugged Andean slopes, Cerro Torre cuts an unmistakable profile against a Patagonia sky. Nearly vertical, Torre was once considered impossible to climb. The first confirmed team to ascend the peak did so in 1970 by creating a ladder-like sequence of anchor bolts. No one would reach the summit without help from these bolts until 2012, and that team dismantled the anchor route on their descent. Though this re-raised the bar for difficulty, several successful summits have occurred since, including some achieved partly by free soloing.

windows-spotlight-12597.jpg.title: Autumn foliage, Lake Pehoé, Torres del Paine National Park, Patagonia, Chile
windows-spotlight-12597.jpg.headline: A Patagonian palette
windows-spotlight-12597.jpg.description: The split coloration of the distant Cuernos del Paine pairs well with the contrasting hues seen here at Lake Pehoé on an orangey autumn day. Fed by glaciers via the Paine River—whose name comes from the Tehuelche word for blue—Pehoé is known for its brilliant turquoise tint, muted here under gray clouds but accented by the brilliant Patagonian fall foliage. As for the Cuernos' double-color job, that big stripe through their middle was stripped by glaciers long ago, leaving a lengthy light-colored patch of bare granite.

windows-spotlight-12599.jpg.title: Patchwork farm fields, Sacramento Valley, Central Valley, United States
windows-spotlight-12599.jpg.headline: California farmin'
windows-spotlight-12599.jpg.description: Much as we think of agriculture as an asset of the United States' heartland, a whole lot of it takes place out here on the West Coast. We're seeing a bird's-eye shot of farm fields in the Sacramento Valley. Home to the state's bustling yet off-the-tourist-path capital, this verdant valley is just one slice of a larger one: the enormous Central Valley sandwiched between California's coastal mountain ranges and the Sierra Nevada. And 'sandwiched' is just the right word, considering this massive fertile basin might be the source of your lunch. Anchored by the Central Valley, California's farming industry produces more than half the United States' fruits, vegetables, and nuts.

windows-spotlight-126.jpg.title: Concrete walls, skyscraper city waterfront
windows-spotlight-126.jpg.headline: Skyscrapers and seaports
windows-spotlight-126.jpg.description: A key port city on the coast of northeastern China, Qingdao sits across the Yellow Sea from Incheon, South Korea. The narrow, distant view in our photo is dominated by sleek glass skyscrapers, marking the city center of this 10 million-strong metropolis. But wander the streets of Qingdao and you'll see smatterings of Romanesque revival architecture. Those are leftovers from the German occupation of the city, which despite only lasting about 16 years (1898-1914) left an enduring stylistic mark.

windows-spotlight-12601.jpg.title: Aragonese Castle of Le Castella, Calabria, Italy
windows-spotlight-12601.jpg.headline: Bulwark on the boot
windows-spotlight-12601.jpg.description: Built over the ruins of an ancient Greek fortification, Le Castella served for centuries as a defense here on Calabria's coast, both from enemy navies and pirate raids. But flying cannonballs and clanking cutlasses are things of the past in this peaceful place near the sole of Italy's boot. Beauty abounds both above and below the water here: A plethora of wildlife ply these seas, protected as the nation's largest marine preserve, and it's a popular place for scuba diving and glass-bottom boat tours.

windows-spotlight-12604.jpg.title: Colorful seaside cottages, Heligoland, Germany
windows-spotlight-12604.jpg.headline: Wheels: Who needs 'em?
windows-spotlight-12604.jpg.description: Overcast skies, treeless hills, and colorful seaside cottages give this island region a Nordic flavor even though it sits substantially south of Scandinavia. Here on the German archipelago of Heligoland, a community of about 1,300 people pack onto the main isle that, when you zoom out, appears sliced in half—while gently sloping hills define the side we're seeing, Heligoland's western edge features sheer cliffs plunging to the North Sea. Including the unpopulated eastern island of Düne, which serves as an airport, Heligoland is just 1.6 square miles in area, and a haven for those who love to hoof it: Save for a few emergency vehicles and bicycle-mounted police, Heligoland is a pedestrian-only zone completely free of wheeled vehicles.

windows-spotlight-12605.jpg.title: Winding river and grassy valley, Héðinsfjörður, Iceland
windows-spotlight-12605.jpg.headline: The fjord that got bored
windows-spotlight-12605.jpg.description: It wasn't so long ago that the uninhabited valley of Héðinsfjörður was every bit as isolated as this shot makes it look. Unlike the neighboring fjords that host the villages of Ólafsfjörður and Siglufjörður, Héðinsfjörður was only accessible by hiking or boating until twin road tunnels were bored through the mountains on each side of it. As it turns out, even boring projects can get a little complicated: The tunnels were first proposed in the 1980s but not completed until 2010, after the two towns merged into one municipality.

windows-spotlight-12606.jpg.title: Tangled Lake Shores, Lake Tengiz, Kazakhstan
windows-spotlight-12606.jpg.headline: Ties to the skies
windows-spotlight-12606.jpg.description: In this sharp shot snapped from the International Space Station, we see the tangled shores of a Kazakhstan salt lake with a historic link to space exploration. In the winter of 1976, Lake Tengiz was the site of an all-hands-on-deck recovery operation when a Soviet Soyuz spacecraft crashed through the ice in sub-zero cold, stranding the crew underwater for 9 hours until they were rescued. That's certainly more action than is typical at this peaceful, wetland-like lake—watch the skies over Tengiz nowadays and you're more likely to see birds coming in for a landing, with more than 300 avian species (including 22 endangered ones) calling this Ramsar site home.

windows-spotlight-12616.jpg.title: Icelandic horse, Iceland
windows-spotlight-12616.jpg.headline: 13 hands and handsome
windows-spotlight-12616.jpg.description: It's hard to tell as this sharp-looking Icelandic horse poses for its portrait, but this breed is barely bigger than a pony, generally standing only 13 or 14 hands high. When the first Icelanders set out around the year 870 from mainland Europe, they brought small, sturdy beasts of burden to help them farm the land—ancestors of the present-day Icelandic horse, weathered over generations by harsh conditions and hard work. The only horse breed allowed in Iceland, these pint-size powerhouses boast a high head count: about 80,000, or one horse for every five people in this sparse Nordic nation.

windows-spotlight-1262.jpg.title: Agave Leaves, Blue-Green
windows-spotlight-1262.jpg.headline: So close you can taste it
windows-spotlight-1262.jpg.description: Cousin to both the asparagus in your fridge and the spider plant on your bookshelf, the agave plant is maybe the most succulent of the succulents. The liquid called aguamiel (Spanish for 'honey water') that fills the plant's core can be cooked down to super-sweet syrup or fermented to create a variety of beverages—yes, including tequila. Though most widely identified with the fat-leafed rosette at its base (seen here in close-up), agave also produces a towering, flowering stalk that's every bit as distinctive. But since its growth stops the plant from storing aguamiel, most cultivated agave is trimmed trunkless.

windows-spotlight-12626.jpg.title: Sunset over Pont d'en Gil, Menorca, Spain
windows-spotlight-12626.jpg.headline: Menorca mood
windows-spotlight-12626.jpg.description: Off the beaten path whether you go by boot, bike, or boat, Pont d'en Gil is a remarkable natural arch on the western edge of Menorca. While hikers can walk the ridgeline over the cutaway passage, passengers on small-to-medium-sized boats can catch a thrill by sailing straight through. Situated on the open Mediterranean with a clear view of the sunset and an ultra-peaceful vibe, Pont d'en Gil is conveniently close to this Spanish isle's largest town, Ciutadella de Menorca.

windows-spotlight-12627.jpg.title: Mykonos Windmills, Mykonos, Cyclades, Greece
windows-spotlight-12627.jpg.headline: Mills of Mykonos
windows-spotlight-12627.jpg.description: Not unlike a visit to the local clubs, these age-old attractions might leave you dizzy: A total of sixteen 16th-century windmills spin within Mykonos' main village. Best known today as a cruise stop with a rowdy nightlife, this Cycladean island is full of markers memorializing its millennia of history. Mykonos was already inhabited when migrants from Athens arrived in the 11th century BCE, and in the intervening centuries has been ruled by the Romans, Byzantines, Venetians (who built the windmills), Ottomans, and finally by modern Greece. Quite the wide geopolitical palette for a place where practically everything is painted white or blue.

windows-spotlight-1263.jpg.title: Svartifoss waterfall basalt columns, Vatnajökull National Park, Iceland
windows-spotlight-1263.jpg.headline: Geology meets geometry
windows-spotlight-1263.jpg.description: Svartifoss is one of several Icelandic waterfalls flanked by distinctive hexagon-shaped basalt columns so smooth they're seemingly carved by the Norse gods themselves. OK, they may not have their origins with Odin's kin, but the science behind them is remarkable. Columnar joints are formed as lava flows cool and buckle under stress, with cracks penetrating deep into newly formed rock. The path of least resistance places these cracks at 120-degree intersections. So as the cracks run deeper, their shape averages out to a near-perfect hexagon—exposing neat geometric columns when the rock face eventually shears off.

windows-spotlight-12632.jpg.title: Star trails and mountain reflections, Mont Blanc Massif, French Alps, France
windows-spotlight-12632.jpg.headline: A land of high beauty
windows-spotlight-12632.jpg.description: Chamonix is a hiker's paradise, with mirror lakes reflecting Alpine peaks, plenty of forested foothills, fields that bloom with wildflowers in the summer, and night skies untouched by light pollution. It's also a popular destination for skiers, and its reputation as one of the world's premier winter playgrounds was cemented when it became the first place to host the Winter Olympic Games in 1924. A glance at our image clearly shows what makes the region such a terrific ski spot—incredible mountains abound here where eastern France borders Switzerland. The star attraction (besides all those star trails, of course)? Mont Blanc rises above Chamonix as the highest mountain in the Alps and the 11th most prominent in the world.

windows-spotlight-12633.jpg.title: Cloud trails over Mont Cenis Massif, Graian Alps, France
windows-spotlight-12633.jpg.headline: Under Alpine skies
windows-spotlight-12633.jpg.description: Near the French-Italian border, the massif known as Mont Cenis rises in France's department of Savoie. While not especially lofty, topping out at less than 12,000 feet, this long ridgeline of peaks includes a mountain pass with a long history, linking the Graian and Cottian Alps—named for the long-past provinces of the Roman Empire that once enclosed them. Today, the pass is still important to both regional transport and travel, lying between Grenoble and the Italian city of Turin—both major urban centers of Alpine culture.

windows-spotlight-12636.jpg.title: Springbok in savanna, Madikwe Game Reserve, South Africa
windows-spotlight-12636.jpg.headline: Savanna sprinter
windows-spotlight-12636.jpg.description: A medium-sized antelope, the springbok is native to the dry savannas of southern Africa, where it once migrated in large numbers. Today, springboks mainly live on wildlife preserves and protected areas, like this one seen at the Madikwe Game Reserve in South Africa. Both males and females of this savannah sprinter species feature distinctive harp-shaped horns: Our photo subject is a lady springbok, as evidenced by its shorter, slenderer headwear compared to the hulking horns seen on males.

windows-spotlight-12638.jpg.title: Sunset reflections, Ullíbarri-Gamboa Reservoir, Basque Country, Spain
windows-spotlight-12638.jpg.headline: A Spanish sunset sizzles
windows-spotlight-12638.jpg.description: As a warm sunset glows up the Ullíbarri-Gamboa Reservoir, the scent of red-hot charcoal grills and the sound of popping wine corks cue the start of dinnertime in nearby Vitoria-Gasteiz—a cultural hub for the Basque Country, a historic region split between Spain and France. The Spanish side—known in Basque as Hegoalde—encompasses most of the population and territory, including Vitoria-Gasteiz and metropolitan Bilbao, comprising an autonomous community of Spain. The northern French side, or Iparralde, is much smaller but packs plenty of culture and scenery, from Biarritz to Bayonne and beyond.

windows-spotlight-1264.jpg.title: Lighthouse Sunset Purple Pink Sky Reflection
windows-spotlight-1264.jpg.headline: A bedazzled beacon
windows-spotlight-1264.jpg.description: The dazzling lights outlining this West Coast outpost are a herald of the holiday season in Santa Cruz, California. Typically trotted out for the city's annual Lighted Boat Parade, they've also been known to spread cheer at other times of the year—for example, during spring 2020, when the rise of COVID-19 had everyone in need of a spirit lift. The classic-style beacon they adorn, the Santa Cruz Breakwater Lighthouse, replaced the previous one (an unsightly metal edifice nicknamed the 'water heater') in 1998.

windows-spotlight-12641.jpg.title: Travertine terraces, Skradinski Buk, Krka National Park, Dalmatia, Croatia
windows-spotlight-12641.jpg.headline: A Dalmatian sweet spot
windows-spotlight-12641.jpg.description: This Croatian region is best known for a spotty local dog breed, and perhaps second-best known for the aquamarine waters of its long Adriatic coast. What many don't know about Dalmatia: Its inland holds turquoise-tinted treasures too. Krka National Park is one of several national parks packed into Dalmatia, preserving not saltwater shore but the ecosystem and scenery of the river Krka. Next to this crossing over the Krka, a roiling cascade called Skradinski Buk tumbles over 17 travertine terraces. It's the largest of seven stepped waterfalls throughout the park, and an even more impressive spectacle up close than from here on high.

windows-spotlight-12645.jpg.title: Australian Pelican, Dune-backed estuary, Australia
windows-spotlight-12645.jpg.headline: Here's your bill
windows-spotlight-12645.jpg.description: Among flying birds, the Australian Pelican definitely punches with the heavyweight class, with the biggest males reaching up to 28 pounds. This Down Under pelican variety also boasts a humongous honker, holding the record among all birds for longest bill—the proboscis that won top prize measured at 20 inches long. The bulky beak is a tool of the bird's trade: Like other pelicans, Aussies use the giant pouch on their bill for fishing, either diving to scoop up prey or using their pouch as a sort of dragnet, trawling for fish and crustaceans while wading the shallows.

windows-spotlight-12647.jpg.title: Hooked land spit, Mývatn, Iceland
windows-spotlight-12647.jpg.headline: From eruption to ecosystem
windows-spotlight-12647.jpg.description: The Land of Fire and Ice is also full of water, and not just the ocean that laps its fjord-laced shores. This hooked land spit juts from one of the many odd-shaped islets of Mývatn, a shallow lake in Iceland's north. Lying in the shadow of Krafla, a large volcano, Mývatn was formed by a basaltic eruption about 2,300 years ago, and rootless cones range in size from massive dips to pimple-like raised spots within and around the lake. Not just rockhounds but birders, anglers, and athletes will find paradise here: Dozens of duck species frequent the lake, the trout and salmon fishing is excellent, and a marathon circling Mývatn's shores is held every summer.

windows-spotlight-12648.jpg.title: Skyscrapers reflected at sunset, Jinji Lake, Suzhou, China
windows-spotlight-12648.jpg.headline: Horizons new and old
windows-spotlight-12648.jpg.description: It's easy to overlook Suzhou on the world map given its proximity to famous Shanghai, but this massively modernized city is steeped in history. Founded more than 2,500 years ago, Suzhou today is dominated by skyscrapers on a carefully designed city plan. Its sleek look is based on urban principles pioneered by Singapore, which struck a deal with China to help develop Suzhou in the 1990s. But as with many of China's metropolises, echoes of the past are preserved amid glass and steel, like the ancient water town of Zhouzhuang and more than 50 classical gardens, some almost a thousand years old.

windows-spotlight-12649.jpg.title: Snow-covered North Rim, Grand Canyon National Park, Arizona, United States
windows-spotlight-12649.jpg.headline: Arizona snows
windows-spotlight-12649.jpg.description: The North Rim is one of the only portions of Grand Canyon National Park that gets snow every winter. The snow causes the National Park Service to close the area during winter months, so few visitors get to see in person such incredible views as this. The rim saw an especially short season in 2025, when the Dragon Bravo Fire swept through the region and burned several historic structures, including the North Rim park headquarters. Today, visitors to the rim will witness a forest landscape in recovery as new life rises from the ashes.

windows-spotlight-1265.jpg.title: Red volcanic crater, green lake, Danakil Depression, Ethiopia
windows-spotlight-1265.jpg.headline: A prodigious pit
windows-spotlight-1265.jpg.description: Without these jade waters as a backdrop, you might think we're seeing the site of a meteorite strike on Mars. Nabiyotum Crater has no connection to outer space, though,as its concave cone is the remnant of a collapsed volcano. It's a remarkable adornment to the southern end of Kenya's 180-mile-long Lake Turkana—the world's largest alkaline lake. Set sail northward and you'll pass another volcanic crater, the still-active Central Island, before reaching Ethiopia near the lake's top tip. But look out! Turkana's plethora of wildlife includes a healthy faction of Nile crocodiles.

windows-spotlight-12651.jpg.title: Sawtooth peaks emerging from fog, Cadini di Misurina, Dolomites, Italy
windows-spotlight-12651.jpg.headline: Misurina majesty
windows-spotlight-12651.jpg.description: Northeastern Italy's Dolomite mountain range is a maze of jagged peaks, plunging valleys, and enormous blocks of nearly bare and impossibly rugged dolomite rock. Around and among this geological wonder lie the thick green forests and rambling pastures of the South Tyrol region. To call this landscape picturesque is an understatement. Nearly every square mile is awe-inspiring, but the mountain group known as the Cadini di Misurina grabs attention with its sawtooth peaks and steep slopes cut through by dozens of valleys. While not quite as renowned as the nearby Tre Cime di Lavaredo, the Cadini group still lures shutterbugs and hardy hikers.

windows-spotlight-12655.jpg.title: Sunrise long exposure waves, Tejita Beach, Tenerife, Canary Islands, Spain
windows-spotlight-12655.jpg.headline: First stop: beach
windows-spotlight-12655.jpg.description: Catch a red-eye flight to Tenerife and this could be your first sunrise seen from Canary Islands shores: Tejita Beach is just a stone's throw from the island's largest airport. After this stop, you have a few options: Head northeast on the TF-1 motorway toward the urban capital of Santa Cruz, west to smaller cities like Los Cristianos and Adeje, or north to the foothills of Teide—a large volcano that's the highest point in Spain. Whichever direction you pick, you'll be in Teide's shadow: The massive mount stands smack in the center of Tenerife, with the island's major roads forming a ring around its base.

windows-spotlight-12657.jpg.title: Pyramid of the Magician, Uxmal, Yucatán, Mexico
windows-spotlight-12657.jpg.headline: A pre-Columbian pyramid
windows-spotlight-12657.jpg.description: The name of this ancient Maya city, Uxmal, is thought to come from a term meaning 'thrice built'—which only tells part of the story of the Pyramid of the Magician. Though legend holds that a short-statured yet skilled sorcerer conjured it in a single night, we know that it was really built in not one or three, but at least five phases across four centuries—each adding significant height to the now 115-foot stone structure. While time has worn and weathered them since the last blocks were laid, the ruins of Uxmal are among the best preserved Maya sites in the Yucatán, easily spotted from a distance due to the pyramid's great prominence.

windows-spotlight-12660.jpg.title: Sunlit huts and Geroldsee, Bavarian Alps, Germany
windows-spotlight-12660.jpg.headline: Bavarian bliss
windows-spotlight-12660.jpg.description: Beneath the Wetterstein—a clustered mountain range that includes Germany's highest peak, Zugspitze—thick forests and verdant plains spread through peaceful Bavarian villages.
